articles.title: How India's Industrial Valve and Pump Industry Supports Infrastructure and Manufacturing - IBEF
articles.summary: How India's Industrial Valve and Pump Industry Supports Infrastructure and Manufacturing  IBEF
articles.full_text:
Pumps and industrial valves represent the basic building blocks of today’s modern infrastructure and manufacturing by enabling the efficient movement, regulation and control of liquids, and other process fluids across industrial systems. The pumps enable the transportation of fluids in pipelines and processing units, whereas the valves provide control over the flow of fluids. These products are used across a wide range of industries, including water and wastewater management, power generation, pharmaceuticals, oil and gas, chemicals, mining, food processing, steel, construction among others, where continuous fluid handling is essential for smooth industrial operations.
With the rise in industrialisation and infrastructure development, India requires highly efficient pumps and industrial valves. Government initiatives such as Make in India, Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme, Market Access Initiative (MAI) Scheme, Brand India Engineering Campaign, Jal Jeevan Mission and the expansion of manufacturing under various industrial policies are driving investments across sectors that rely extensively on fluid control equipment.
As per DPIIT, India’s manufacturing industry is set to be one of the key drivers for India’s economic growth in the long term, supported by continued investments in industrial infrastructure, advanced engineering capabilities, and policy-led manufacturing initiatives. India has become the most important manufacturing destination for engineering products because of the presence of a robust network of manufacturers, MSMEs, and export-based industries.
India's industrial valve and pump industry was valued at Rs. 19,911.10 crore (US$ 2,284.50 million) in 2025 and is projected to reach Rs. 34,399.04 crore (US$ 3,711.80 million) by 2034. The industrial valves and pumps industry is a key contributor to India's engineering and capital goods sector, supporting the development of infrastructure and the efficient operation of manufacturing and process industries. The sector includes a diverse network of large manufacturers, micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), and engineering firms operating in both domestic and international markets. India manufactures a wide range of industrial pumps, valves, and flow control systems used in water and wastewater management, oil and gas, power generation, chemical, pharmaceutical, mining, and food processing industries, showing the growth of India's industrial base.
India's engineering exports showed steady growth within the last decade, from around Rs. 4.28 lakh crore (US$ 70 billion) in FY15 to a record-high Rs. 10.82 lakh crore (US$ 122.43 billion) in FY26, thus confirming the increasing manufacturing capabilities of India and its growing competitiveness. Engineering sector remains the main exporter in India, which accounts for almost 28% of India's merchandise exports. Moreover, the sector showed record growth in exports for three consecutive years, when the exports amounted to Rs. 9.05 lakh crore (US$ 109.30 billion) in FY24, to Rs. 10.09 lakh crore (US$ 116.67 billion) in FY25 and Rs. 10.82 lakh crore (US$ 122.43 billion) in FY26.
The growth has been supported by government initiatives such as the Market Access Initiative (MAI) Scheme, Brand India Engineering Campaign, and the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme, among others, along with expanded market access through Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) with the United Arab Emirates, Australia, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) countries. Further strengthening the export ecosystem, the Export Promotion Mission, with an outlay of Rs. 25,060 crore (US$ 2.65 billion) for 2025-31, aims to promote exports through digital trade facilitation, improved market access, and enhanced support for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
As India progresses further with investment in infrastructure, manufacturing industries, energy, and urban developments, there is expected to be increasing demand for industrial valves and pumps. Along with the government policies favouring domestic manufacture and export of engineering, the industry is set to strengthen its position in aiding India's infrastructure growth, industrial competitiveness, and engineering supply chain.
Government policy has played a crucial role in strengthening India's industrial valve and pump industry by promoting domestic manufacturing, accelerating infrastructure development and enhancing the competitiveness of the engineering sector.
The following factors are supporting the growth of India's industrial valve and pump industry, driven by increasing investments in infrastructure, manufacturing, water management and energy projects.
India's industrial valves and pumps industry is well positioned for sustained growth, supported by increasing investments in infrastructure, manufacturing, and green energy projects. In addition, the establishment of new manufacturing facilities, including semiconductor fabrication plants, is expected to drive demand for industrial valves and pumps across process manufacturing and utility applications. Increasing investments in the areas of water supply networks, sewage treatment, industrial corridors, electricity production, and construction of smart cities are likely to create steady demand for advanced solutions of fluid handling and flow control systems. Government initiatives to strengthen domestic manufacturing, supported by rising engineering exports, are enhancing India's position as a global manufacturing hub and creating new export opportunities for Indian manufacturers.
Another key factor that will contribute to the growth of the industrial valve and pump industry will be the rise in the application of smart manufacturing, energy-saving solutions, and digital industrial technologies. With the increasing need of industrial facilities to improve their performance by implementing new technologies, the demand for intelligent valve and pump systems, which will be equipped with IoT monitoring, predictive maintenance, and automation technologies, will rise. Further, the development of emerging segments such as green hydrogen, water recycling, desalination, renewable energy, and process manufacturing will create new market opportunities.
Supported by continued policy initiatives, infrastructure investments and technological innovation, India's industrial valve and pump industry is poised to play an increasingly strategic role in strengthening the country's industrial competitiveness. By enabling efficient resource management, reliable industrial operations and sustainable infrastructure development, the sector will continue to support India's vision of becoming a globally competitive manufacturing and engineering powerhouse.
The industry is an integral part of India's engineering and capital goods sector, supplying critical equipment for infrastructure, manufacturing, energy, and process industries. It also supports domestic production and engineering exports.
Rapid urbanisation is increasing investments in water supply networks, sewage treatment plants, commercial buildings, and industrial infrastructure. These developments are driving the demand for industrial valves and pumps across municipal and industrial applications.
Industrial valves and pumps help regulate fluid flow, maintain system pressure, and optimise energy consumption. Their use improves process efficiency, reduces operational downtime, and enhances the reliability of industrial systems.
The aftermarket, including maintenance, repair, replacement, and refurbishment services, plays an important role in extending equipment life and improving operational reliability. Growing industrial activity is expected to support demand for aftermarket services.
Growing engineering, exports are creating opportunities for domestic manufacturers to expand their presence in international markets. Increasing product quality, manufacturing capabilities, and compliance with global standards are supporting the industry's export competitiveness.

articles.title: GCCs in India: From Call Centres and BPOs to Global Innovation Hubs - Youth Incorporated Magazine
articles.summary: GCCs in India: From Call Centres and BPOs to Global Innovation Hubs  Youth Incorporated Magazine
articles.full_text:
Global Capability Centres (GCCs) were first established in India in 1985. Texas Instruments set up its first GCC in Bengaluru, followed by Citicorp Overseas Software Limited [COSL] in Pune in the same year.
On September 30, 2026, DoorDash opened a hub in Hyderabad with 500 employees, planning to make it a firm with 3000 employees in the next 2 years. It also had a small data and software analytics office set up in 2021 in Pune when it acquired Chowbotics.
DoorDash is not launching its company in India. They are just using this centre as an offshore facility to handle Customer Experience & Integrity (CXI) through general and administrative teams. This is their 3rd centre, followed by Arizona and Mexico.
DoorDash is joining companies such as Costco, McDonald's, Charles Schwab, Marriott and Southwest Airlines [amongst another 430-500] that have recently expanded their GCC operations/presence in Hyderabad. And it is definitely not the only one.
Starbucks recently announced that it will establish a GCC in Chennai, creating almost 800 jobs. It plans to expand and eventually bring third-party work in-house.
With that announcement, we have the right to ask: why are global companies increasingly building key parts of their operations in India?
What is GCC?
To perform functions and execute operations for their global business, multinational companies develop offshore offices in other countries. These offices are company-owned or company-controlled. The primary reason for this is to obtain talented individuals from talent-rich hubs like India at a lower cost. It speeds up the digital transformation.
The employees are hired to control internal operations like software engineering, IT support, finance, human resources and legal compliance. And other than the basic back-office tasks, they also have teams for advanced research, AI development, data analytics, and product design.
Before GCC, companies had to hire third-party vendors, like outsourcing them for certain tasks and services. These companies were handling sensitive code and data of the company while also serving competitors. There was a huge risk of leaks. They were also expensive, with fees added to the pay of workers. Even then, they were just focused on finishing the contracts, with zero loyalty.
GCC bridges this gap. The workers, codes, information, budgets- everything is under the company's direct control. Employees are made to sign the NDA; they care for the company, they are accustomed to the company’s culture, and they work for long-term success. And now, moving from the traditional setup, India's GCC story is increasingly about ownership and strategic capability rather than just lower operating costs.
There is a simple distinction between a Call Center/BPO and a Global Capability Centre. Call Centres/BPOs just fulfil a function, whereas a GCC runs an entire offshore business operation or capability hub. So it's not just simple customer service, calls, and support, but it's more of high-skilled professional and technical roles in the field of IT, software, finance, analytics, R&D, engineering, HR, legal, cybersecurity, etc.
How Did India Become A GCC Hub?
The Numbers: How Big Is India's GCC Industry Now?
Why Are Companies Choosing India?
India holds the highest number of GCCs in the world, holding over 55% of the global market share. Why? Because:
- Talent: Indian professionals account for 28% of the global STEM workforce and 23% of global software engineering talent. We have a large pool of talented and distinguished individuals.
- Cost: Initially, every company wanted Indian workers because it was cheaper. Data entry and payroll were done by Indians at lower prices. But currently, India is looked upon as a centre for skilled individuals, and companies are no longer concerned about cost-cutting.
- Technology Ecosystem: India already has an established ecosystem for AI, Cloud, IT, Fintech, Cybersecurity, Engineering and Data. This makes it very easy for companies, cutting their time and energy compared to starting from scratch.
- Scale: India not only has specialised talent, but it also allows these companies to build their own specialised centres of excellence. This ensures that even though the companies are in a foreign land, everything is to their satisfaction.
The advantage is no longer simply that India can do the same work for less; increasingly, companies are coming to India because they can find capabilities that are difficult to scale elsewhere.
Why do GCCs Matter to India?
As youth, we are often looked upon as the backbone of the economy. A country’s development is highly based on the growth and upbringing of its youth. GCCs matter to India for this specific reason. An average Indian should care about these because:
- Economic Impact: GCCs are a $100 billion ecosystem. They create millions of skilled jobs for the country’s youth. They are a source of foreign multinational investments. Setting up these centres also accounts for the increase in demand for commercial real estate. In addition to this, GCCs can create growth in technology and professional services.
- Talent Impact: GCCs are now working beyond the traditional services of data entry, payrolls and basic IT jobs. They create opportunities in the field of engineering, finance, IT, analytics, cybersecurity, product management, global leadership, operations, and R&D. The demand for this in the country makes it possible for the younger generation to develop and grow in these fields.
- City-level Impact: GCCs are not just confined to Bengaluru. Other cities like Hyderabad, Delhi, Pune, Mumbai, Chennai, Coimbatore, Kochi, Ahmedabad, Jaipur, Indore and Bhubaneswar are also emerging as hubs. These cities are seeing a wave of announcements, and this demonstrates the continuing geographic spread.
What GCCs Want From India's Next Generation of Talent?
As the GCCs continue to evolve in India, the experts suggest that the coming generation can take full advantage of this opportunity by making sure they have the following skills:
- You need to have basic business and technology knowledge. It is fine if you cannot code, but you should have hands-on experience with AI, digital transformation, data and automation to some extent.
- Instead of just executing instructions, you should be a capable strategic thinker, working on global business platforms.
- You should have the ability to understand data and analyse it to make correct decisions.
- You should know how to use AI effectively for different fields like marketing, finance, operations, HR, etc.
- You should be a team player. Cross-functional management is important as many different teams require coordination under one roof.
- You should be well-versed with the stakeholders globally, and your communications with them should be impactful and influential.
- You need to be able to adapt to new technology quickly and be a problem-solver instead of a process follower.
The Future: Where Are GCCs Heading?
With the fast and furious emergence of AI (Artificial Intelligence), the threat to menial jobs is alarming. AI in GCCs can automate repetitive work, reducing the requirement for certain transactional roles, changing existing job descriptions, and increasing productivity.
While this may sound like a negative, on the positive side, AI is creating demand for AI/ML engineers, data scientists, AI product managers, cybersecurity specialists, AI governance professionals, cloud engineers, and domain experts.
These are some established GCC’s in India: JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, BlackRock, Wells Fargo, HSBC, Deutsche Bank, Barclays, Citigroup, American Express, Standard Chartered, MUFG, UBS, Fidelity and Franklin Templeton. Further added more than 100 GCCs expansions in FY2026, and new entrants included companies such as Charles Schwab, BASF, eBay and Revolut.
India's GCC story is no longer simply about how many companies are setting up offices here. The more important question is what those offices are being trusted to do. If the current shift continues, India's GCCs could move further from executing instructions created elsewhere to designing products, developing technologies and making decisions with global impact. For young professionals, that could mean a job market where the most valuable skills are not limited to coding or traditional IT, but extend to AI, creativity, domain expertise, problem-solving and global business understanding.

articles.title: Silicon Wafer Manufacturing Plant Setup in India - IMARC Group
articles.summary: Silicon Wafer Manufacturing Plant Setup in India  IMARC Group
articles.full_text:
Silicon wafers are the thin, precisely sliced discs and squares on which solar cells and computer chips are built. India has rapidly become a major assembler of solar modules and is now building cell capacity, but almost all of the wafers those cells need are still imported. With the government extending its approved-manufacturer framework to ingots and wafers from June 2028, and semiconductor fabs taking shape in several states, a Silicon Wafer Manufacturing Plant Setup in India has moved from a distant ambition to a strategic, policy-backed opportunity. It is, however, one of the most capital- and technology-intensive projects in the manufacturing sector, and it rewards investors who plan for scale, energy, and technical depth.
This guide focuses mainly on solar-grade monocrystalline ingots and wafers, where India's near-term demand is largest, and also explains how semiconductor-grade wafers differ. Investment depends on capacity, crystal growth technology, and wafer format. For a solar ingot-and-wafer plant of roughly 1 to 10 GW a year, the Silicon Wafer Manufacturing Plant Cost ranges from about INR 600 crore to INR 6,000 crore, while semiconductor-grade wafer facilities require separate, specialised investment. Polysilicon and electricity together dominate operating cost, so feedstock sourcing and power pricing are the decisions that shape profitability. At healthy utilisation, a well-run solar wafer plant can deliver a net profit margin of 8 to 15% and an IRR of 13 to 20%, with payback typically within 5 to 7 years.
This guide is written for investors trying to understand how to start a Silicon Wafer manufacturing plant in India. It covers the product types and their markets, the demand outlook, the production flow, machinery and raw materials, site and infrastructure planning, a detailed cost and financial breakdown, the approvals involved, and how a DPR turns all of this into a plan that lenders can evaluate.
| Key Facts | Details | 
|---|---|
| India Silicon Wafer Market (2025) | USD 1.14 Billion | 
| Forecast (2034) | USD 1.65 Billion, 4.04% CAGR (2026–2034) | 
| Solar Wafer Import Dependence | Close to 100% of demand currently imported | 
| Policy Trigger | ALMM List-III for ingots and wafers from 1 June 2028 | 
| Indicative Total Investment | INR 600–6,000 Crore (1–10 GW solar ingot-wafer) | 
| Typical Payback Period | 5–7 Years | 
The snapshot captures both the size of the gap and the policy tailwind. India's solar module and cell industries have scaled rapidly, but wafers remain almost entirely imported, and the coming ALMM requirement for wafers will create protected domestic demand for projects bid after it takes effect. The challenge is that global wafer production is dominated by very large, low-cost producers, so new Indian plants must be built at scale, with modern technology and competitive power, to succeed. The sections below work through these choices.
Indicative Project Cost in India (2026)
| Parameter | Value | 
|---|---|
| Product Range | n-type and p-type mono wafers in large formats; optional semiconductor-grade | 
| Total Project Investment | INR 600 – 6,000 Crore (1–10 GW solar ingot-wafer) | 
| Payback Period | 5 – 7 Years | 
| Net Profit Margin | 8 – 15% | 
| IRR | 13 – 20% | 
| Preferred States | Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Odisha, Maharashtra | 
| Key Approvals | SPCB consents, Factory License, EHT power connection, gas and chemical storage licenses, ALMM List-III | 
| Key Requirement | Low-cost reliable power and assured polysilicon supply | 
These ranges provide a realistic frame for early planning, but actual returns depend heavily on polysilicon prices, power tariffs, wafer yields, global wafer pricing, and the timing of ALMM List-III. A site-specific Silicon Wafer Feasibility Report narrows each of these assumptions to your chosen capacity, technology, and location.
Table of Contents
Silicon wafer manufacturing starts with ultra-pure polysilicon, which is melted and grown into a single large crystal, or ingot, using the Czochralski method. The ingot is then cut into shorter lengths, shaped into bricks for solar wafers or ground into cylinders for semiconductor wafers, and sliced into very thin wafers with diamond wire saws. Solar wafers are cleaned, inspected, and sorted for cell makers, while semiconductor wafers go through further lapping, etching, polishing, and cleaning to reach near-perfect flatness and purity.
Commercially, wafers sit at a pivotal point in two strategic value chains. A well-run Silicon Wafer Manufacturing Plant producing solar wafers can supply India's rapidly growing cell makers, including integrated module producers who need domestic wafers to meet future ALMM rules. Semiconductor-grade wafers serve chip fabs and research institutions, but require far higher purity, tighter tolerances, and qualification by fab customers, making them a distinct and more demanding business.
The Main Silicon Wafer Product Types
Choosing which wafers to produce is the most consequential decision, because it defines the technology, investment scale, and customers:
| Wafer Type | Description | Key Property | Primary Demand | 
|---|---|---|---|
| n-type Mono Solar Wafers | Phosphorus-doped monocrystalline | High efficiency, low degradation | TOPCon and HJT cell makers | 
| p-type Mono Solar Wafers | Boron- or gallium-doped mono | Lower cost, mature technology | PERC cell lines (declining) | 
| Large-Format Solar Wafers | 182 mm, 210 mm, and rectangular sizes | Higher module power | New cell lines | 
| Semiconductor Prime Wafers | Polished, ultra-flat wafers | Extreme purity and flatness | Chip fabs | 
| Test & Reclaim Wafers | Lower-specification or reprocessed wafers | Cost-effective for process tests | Fabs and R&D labs | 
Product choice shapes the entire project. Solar wafer plants focus on high-throughput crystal pullers and diamond wire slicing, with n-type wafers now the industry standard for TOPCon and HJT cells. Semiconductor wafer plants add precision grinding, lapping, polishing, and ultra-clean handling, with far longer customer qualification cycles. For most Indian investors today, a large-scale n-type solar wafer plant, ideally linked to cell capacity, is the practical entry point.
Key Growth Drivers in the Indian Market
Demand for domestically made wafers is being driven by a combination of industrial growth and policy:
India-Specific Market Opportunity
| Segment | India Market Context | Manufacturing Role | 
|---|---|---|
| Integrated Solar Manufacturers | Backward integration into wafers | Captive n-type wafer supply | 
| Independent Cell Makers | Need ALMM-compliant wafers from 2028 | Merchant wafer sales | 
| Government-Linked Projects | Domestic content requirements | Certified, traceable wafers | 
| Semiconductor Fabs | Early-stage domestic ecosystem | Future prime and test wafers | 
| Exports | Buyers diversifying away from single-country supply | Traceable, non-Chinese wafers | 
The strongest near-term opportunity lies in large-scale n-type solar wafer production linked to cell capacity, either within an integrated group or through long-term supply contracts with independent cell makers. As the semiconductor ecosystem matures, test and reclaim wafers may offer a stepping stone toward prime semiconductor wafers for investors with deep technical partners.
Understanding the flow helps you plan machinery, utilities, and where yield and cost are decided. Wafer production combines high-temperature crystal growth with precision mechanical processing and ultra-clean handling. Crystal quality, slicing precision, and breakage control together determine how many good wafers each kilogram of polysilicon yields.
The Silicon Wafer Manufacturing Process Flow
The sequence below reflects a typical solar-grade monocrystalline ingot and wafer plant. Semiconductor wafer plants follow the same crystal growth principle but add grinding, lapping, etching, polishing, and advanced cleaning after slicing.
| Unit Operation | Key Activity | 
|---|---|
| Polysilicon Receipt & Preparation | Feedstock inspected, sorted, and cleaned | 
| Crucible Charging | Polysilicon and dopant loaded into quartz crucible | 
| Melting & Crystal Growth | Single-crystal ingot grown in Czochralski puller | 
| Ingot Cooling & Inspection | Ingot removed and checked for quality | 
| Cropping & Squaring | Ingot cut into lengths and shaped into bricks | 
| Grinding & Chamfering | Brick surfaces and corners finished | 
| Diamond Wire Slicing | Bricks sliced into thin wafers | 
| Degluing & Cleaning | Wafers separated and cleaned | 
| Inspection & Sorting | Thickness, flatness, defects, and resistivity checked | 
| Packing & Dispatch | Wafers packed in protective boxes and shipped | 
Two factors decide profitability across this flow. The first is silicon yield: polysilicon is the largest material cost, and losses in crystal growth, cropping, and slicing kerf directly raise cost per wafer, so continuous-feed pullers, thin diamond wire, and thin wafers are key levers. The second is energy, because crystal pullers run continuously at very high temperatures, making electricity one of the largest costs; access to low-cost, reliable power, including renewable supply, can decide whether a plant is globally competitive.
The main input is high-purity polysilicon, supported by quartz crucibles, dopants, diamond wire, process gases such as argon, graphite hot-zone parts, and cleaning chemicals. Because polysilicon dominates material cost and must meet stringent purity standards, a secure, qualified supply is central to project planning.

articles.summary: India’s manufacturing ambition – Fiscal policy perspective  kpmg.com
articles.full_text:
For much of the past three decades since 1991, the global investment narrative around India was straightforward: a large consumer market with rising income where global products could be sold. Increasingly, however, that narrative is changing. India is no longer positioning itself simply as a destination where multinational corporations sell products or source talent. It is making a more ambitious proposition; it wants to be the location where multinational companies manufacture and sell to the world. The economy grew 7.7 per cent in FY2025-26i, and 7.8 per cent in Q1 of FY26-27 despite all odds and gross FDI inflows for last year reached a record of about USD95 billion.
Across the world, governments and corporations are committing unprecedented capital towards semiconductors, artificial intelligence infrastructure, data centres, clean energy, electric mobility, advanced manufacturing and supply-chain diversification. India is seeking to position itself as a promising alternative in this super capex cycle, not merely as a domestic consumption-based market, but as a location where global companies can invest, manufacture, innovate and serve international demand.
Make in India (2014)ii made manufacturing a national priority and was accompanied by step-by-step liberalisation of FDI rules in several sectors. Atmanirbhar Bharat (2020)iii added a second goal: domestic capability and supply-chain resilience in strategic sectors, supported by incentives linked to output as compared to past protectionist measures. Since then, the Government also focused on what a factory needs beyond its own gates. PM Gati Shakti and the National Logistics Policy bring infrastructure planning across ministries onto one platform. The National Single Window System brings Central and State approvals into one portal. The National Manufacturing Mission announced in the 2025-26 Budget is being taken forward by an inter-ministerial committee.iv The 2026-27 Budget went further, prioritising seven strategic and frontier sectors, including semiconductors, electronics components, biopharma, rare earths and capital goods.v The manufacturing ambition is also increasingly extending from 'Make in India' towards 'Make in India, Make for the World', with greater emphasis on exports, global competitiveness and participation in global value chains.vi
In recent years, India has introduced a series of tax reforms and incentives aimed at improving certainty, reducing friction and aligning its fiscal framework with long-term capital deployment.

articles.title: Mecca Pact activated: Pakistan, Turkey to rapidly deploy troops to Saudi Arabia - India Today
articles.summary: Mecca Pact activated: Pakistan, Turkey to rapidly deploy troops to Saudi Arabia  India Today
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey have moved to operationalise the Mecca Pact with rapid force deployment arrangements. The step comes amid persistent security threats to the kingdom from the Houthis and signals a tighter collective defence posture.
The Mecca Pact was activated on Monday, with Pakistan and Turkey agreeing to move towards the rapid deployment of troops and military capabilities to Saudi Arabia under their new mutual defence alliance.
The decision was announced after an emergency meeting of the Strategic-Political and Defense Committee of the Makkah Alliance for Defense in Riyadh on October 5. The move comes amid continuing attacks and security threats facing Saudi Arabia, including those linked to the Iran-aligned Houthis.
The joint statement shared by Pakistan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the committee had decided to “move immediately to the practical implementation” of collective defence commitments and take necessary measures to provide agreed military forces and capabilities for their rapid deployment in Saudi Arabia.
MILITARY FORCES TO BE DEPLOYED UNDER AGREED TERMS
The deployment will be carried out in accordance with approved arrangements and the national laws of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey, the statement said.
The move is aimed at strengthening military readiness, improving integration between the three countries and enhancing their collective ability to respond to threats.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey also condemned what they described as attempts to target Mecca and Madina, along with continuing attacks on Saudi cities and civilian and economic facilities.
The three countries praised the Saudi Armed Forces for their vigilance and readiness and their role in protecting the kingdom’s security and territorial integrity.
SENIOR MILITARY, DEFENCE OFFICIALS ATTEND RIYADH MEETING
The high-level meeting was attended by senior defence and military officials from all three countries. Turkey’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Defence Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu represented Ankara.
Pakistan was represented by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar, Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif. Saudi Arabia was represented by Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Chief of General Staff General Fayyadh bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili.
Pakistan’s retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood, who has been appointed Secretary-General of the Mecca defence pact, also took part in the meeting.
PAKISTANI GENERAL NAMED FIRST SECRETARY-GENERAL
The committee appointed Pakistan’s Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood (Ret.) as the first Secretary-General of the Makkah Alliance for Defense for a three-year term.
The three countries said the security of each member was an integral part of their collective security. They stressed that implementing the Mecca Agreement for Joint Defense demonstrated their commitment to collective defence and would strengthen deterrence.
HOUTHI THREATS ADD TO REGIONAL TENSIONS
The activation of the pact comes as Saudi Arabia faces a sustained campaign from the Houthis, including attacks the group says have targeted the kingdom’s energy infrastructure.
The latest move marks a significant step in military cooperation between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey, with the three countries signalling a coordinated response to threats against the kingdom.
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7. Under the pact, an armed attack on any one of the three would be treated as an attack on all three.
Since then, the countries have worked to establish the institutions needed to make the pact operational. Their foreign and defence ministers and military chiefs met in Istanbul in August, while the military chiefs held further discussions in Riyadh on September 25.

President Masoud Pezeshkian accepted Mohsen Paknejad’s resignation on Sunday and appointed NIOC chief Hamid Bovard as acting oil minister, according to Reuters. The president’s office said Paknejad had asked to resign for personal reasons “a long time ago” and Pezeshkian had previously rejected his request.
Bovard takes over with Washington trying to cut off Iran’s remaining oil exports. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Saturday that Iran had no oil shipments remaining at sea and would generate zero oil revenue this week, according to Anadolu. Iran’s central bank governor said in August that the country’s oil exports had effectively fallen to zero.
Just hours before his resignation was announced, Paknejad was quoted as saying revenues from oil already sold were still reaching Iran and would continue, according to Reuters.
Bovard is already under U.S. sanctions. The U.S. Treasury designated him in February 2025 for operating in Iran’s petroleum sector as part of sanctions targeting Iran’s oil industry and its so-called shadow fleet. At the time, the Treasury identified Bovard as both Iran’s deputy oil minister and NIOC managing director.
Iran is also struggling with fuel supply at home. The National reports that the country faces a gasoline deficit of roughly 10 million liters per day. Tehran raised the price of gasoline purchased above the subsidized monthly quota last month after shortages and queues at filling stations.
Bovard, 62, has headed NIOC since 2024 and previously ran the National Iranian South Oil Company and Iranian Offshore Oil Company. He has spent much of his career in oilfield operations.
The pressure on oil revenues is feeding into Iran’s wider financial crisis. The rial fell to a record low of about 2.688 million to the dollar last week, while inflation has climbed above 70%, according to Reuters.
Paknejad had run the Oil Ministry since August 2024. His departure leaves Bovard responsible for maintaining production and finding a route to market for Iranian crude while Washington tries to prevent those barrels from leaving the country.

articles.full_text:
DELHI, India – Governor Greg Gianforte today continued Montana’s trade mission to India, meeting with technology companies, investors, manufacturers, and business leaders to promote Montana’s growing industries and attract new investment to the Treasure State to create jobs for Montanans.
“As our conversations continue in India, we are expanding opportunity for our leading industries beyond agriculture and making meaningful connections with successful entrepreneurs and business leaders ready to partner on the innovations of tomorrow,” Gov. Gianforte said. “We’re showing investors and businesses in India why the Treasure State should be part of their next big idea.
Gov. Gianforte, First Landy Gianforte meeting with Nasscom in New Delhi
Gov. Gianforte began the day at a business roundtable hosted by Nasscom, India’s leading technology industry association, meeting with startups and large companies working in artificial intelligence, quantum computing, semiconductors, and other emerging technologies.
Nasscom represents over 3,000 companies of India's $315 billion technology industry that works across industry, government, and academia. Aligning interests in Montana, the governor and trade mission delegates highlighted the state’s established optics, photonics, and quantum ecosystem and opportunities for Indian technology companies to collaborate with Montana businesses, researchers, and universities.
Montana has the highest per-capita concentrations of optics and photonics companies and research institutions in the United States. Through Montana State University (MSU), the state has invested in building an applied quantum ecosystem around QCORE, providing researchers and industry with hands-on access to multiple quantum computing technologies and test infrastructure. In the meeting, MSU President Brock Tessman noted how these technologies are available to private companies interested in exploring collaborative research and prototype opportunities.
Supporting Montana’s growing photonics industry, the state in 2024 was designated as one of 31 inaugural regional technology and innovation hubs in the U.S., establishing the federally designated Headwaters Tech Hub which received approximately $41 million in federal funding to build out a regional photonics product-development supply chain and strengthen Montana’s capacity to move new technologies from research to commercialization.
Montana’s broader technology industry is also driving economic growth. In a new report released by the Montana High Tech Business Alliance, the sector generates nearly $8 billion in annual revenue, contributes approximately $4.4 billion to Montana’s economy, and supports more than 38,000 jobs across the state.
Later in the day, the governor joined the Indian Venture and Alternate Capital Association (IVCA) for a working lunch with Indian fund managers and investors focused on Montana’s bioscience, agricultural technology, deep tech, and photonics industries. With over 490 members, IVCA has contributed a combined investment exceeding $350 billion.
Approaching the discussion based on his experience as an entrepreneur, Gov. Gianforte and the delegation focused on connecting capital with Montana entrepreneurs, researchers, universities, and emerging companies to help new technologies move from research to commercialization. The group had a particular interest in the tech industry, bioscience, and the opportunities that exist with Montana’s Right to Try law for investments in pharmaceutical clinical trials.
In 2025, Gov. Gianforte announced Montana was ranked as the best state for business startups. According to data reported by Entrepreneur Media, Montana was ranked number one with the highest score for the total number of startups in the state, the number of startups per capita, and the 10-year survival rate of startups.
Montana’s growing innovation economy is also gaining national recognition. In December 2025, Bozeman was selected as the location for the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s Northwest Frontier Community Engagement Office, providing entrepreneurs, researchers, and inventors throughout Montana and the region greater access to resources related to patents, trademarks, and intellectual property.
The governor concluded the day in Delhi with the U.S.-India Business Council (USIBC), meeting with business leaders to discuss biotechnology, advanced manufacturing, critical and emerging technologies, supply chains, and opportunities for Indian companies to invest in Montana.
During the discussion, the governor highlighted Montana’s strong economic environment, with the state recently ranking as the fifth-fastest-growing economy in the nation. From 2021 to 2025, Montana’s real gross domestic product grew 16.1 percent, outpacing national economic growth during the same period.
The delegation also highlighted Montana’s strengths in energy, agriculture, and aerospace, industries where Montana and India already share opportunities for greater cooperation.
Agriculture is a $6.22 billion industry in Montana, and the state is the nation’s leading producer of peas, lentils, and chickpeas. In 2025, India purchased approximately $3.3 million in Montana pulse crops.
Aerospace is another growing connection. In 2025, India purchased approximately $6.9 million in commercial aircraft parts from Montana, an all-time high and making India Montana’s sixth-largest market for the product. Boeing has operated a manufacturing facility in Helena for years, producing complex titanium and hard-metal components for aircraft including the 787-10 and 777X.
Montana is also seeing significant new investment in advanced manufacturing. Janicki Industries is developing an $800 million manufacturing campus in Great Falls, expected to create approximately 1,000 jobs within five years and more than 2,000 jobs at full build out. Montana’s bioscience sector is similarly attracting global investment. GlaxoSmithKline has invested more than $100 million to expand manufacturing capabilities at its Hamilton facility, where it produces components for vaccine adjuvant systems.
“We didn’t come to India just to exchange business cards. We came to build business,” Gov. Gianforte said. “A new investment, a new research partnership, or a Montana company reaching a new market means more opportunity back home.”
The governor tomorrow will continue his trade mission in Bengaluru.

articles.full_text:
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer recently said an agreement was not imminent, as Washington and New Delhi continue to work through unresolved issues.
Trade negotiations between India and the US are “still ongoing” even as both sides have “reached a plateau” beyond which further give-and-take “might be very, very difficult,” Union finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday, days after US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said an agreement was “not imminent.”
Speaking on India’s approach to the next generation of trade agreements at the Munich Leaders Meeting (MLM), organised by the Munich Security Conference in New Delhi, Sitharaman cited the India-EU free trade agreement concluded on January 2026 as an example of a mutually beneficial deal in which both sides respected each other’s sensitivities.
Also read: Next-Generation GST and India’s next growth phase | Nirmala Sitharaman writes for HT
Sitharaman says India-US trade talks remain underway
Asked whether this would serve as a template for other negotiations, particularly with the US, Sitharaman said the India-US agreement “is yet to get finalised” and has been “a hard and very rigorously negotiated agreement”.
“The agreement’s negotiations are still ongoing, although we’d like to believe that both the sides have reached a plateau, beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult,” she said.
“But maybe, if there are rooms to operate from, both sides would do it,” she added, indicating that New Delhi and Washington were looking for common ground. India, however, maintains that there is no single template for trade negotiations as economic realities vary across countries and regions.
Also read: Trump mistakes Brazil for India, says 125 million voted today in 'India's Presidential Election'
Greer says India-US deal is not imminent
Sitharaman’s remarks came days after Greer said at a press conference following the G20 Trade Ministers’ meeting in Milwaukee that he did not think there was “something imminent” on a trade deal with India. He said the two sides had identified “the universe of items” that were sticking points.
Greer also said US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi may have another phone call “very soon” to assess progress on the trade deal.
According to trade experts, uncertainties created by Washington’s frequent trade measures and the use of tariffs as a negotiating tool are major hurdles to signing an interim bilateral trade agreement (BTA). The two countries had issued a joint statement on February 7 outlining a framework for an interim BTA.
India seeks competitive access for exporters
However, the agreement was not signed after the US Supreme Court invalidated the legal basis for the preferential tariff mechanism Washington had offered, the experts said. India is now awaiting a preferential tariff framework that provides competitive access for its exporters vis-a-vis competing countries, they added.
Sitharaman also said the balance of bilateral trade between India and the US was in India’s favour and that Washington’s concerns over its trade deficit could be addressed through negotiations rather than the “weaponization” of tariffs.
Also read: Deepening the India-US defence partnership | US Ambassador Gor writes for HT
India cites China trade deficit in tariff argument
Citing China, with which both the US and India run large trade deficits, she said negotiations were the best way to address trade imbalances rather than using tariffs or other measures.
“Tariff was an instrument of negotiation. And tariff had a certain framework within which you will apply it,” Sitharaman said. In a reference to India’s trade deficit with China, she said: “So, I can probably take the same position, can I not?... But no, you can’t. You will have to talk it out. You will have to negotiate.”
Bilateral merchandise trade between India and China stood at $151.1 billion in 2025-26, with India recording a trade deficit of $112.6 billion.
In 2025, total China-US bilateral trade was $414.7 billion, with the US recording a trade deficit of about $202.7 billion. India, however, reported a trade surplus of $34.4 billion with the US in 2025-26, narrowing from a surplus of $40.89 billion in 2024-25.

articles.title: India-US trade talks hit 'plateau' as room for concessions narrows, says Nirmala Sitharaman - The New Indian Express
articles.summary: India-US trade talks hit 'plateau' as room for concessions narrows, says Nirmala Sitharaman  The New Indian Express
articles.full_text:
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Monday said negotiations for the India-US trade agreement remain ongoing, but both sides appear to have reached a “plateau”, leaving limited scope for further concessions.
Speaking at the Munich Security Conference, Sitharaman said there could still be room for movement if both countries identified areas where compromises were possible.
“The agreement’s negotiations are still ongoing, although we like to believe that both sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult. But maybe, if there is room to operate from, both sides would do it,” she said.
Sitharaman said a predominant feature of India-US trade relations is the trade imbalance in India's favour, with the US seeking to reduce its deficit.
“Ultimately, the deficit is there on their side, or the balance is unfavourable for the US, so they would want to reduce that imbalance,” she said, adding that the US would seek to compensate for what it believes it has lost over the years.
Drawing a comparison with India’s trade relationship with China, Sitharaman said trade imbalances have traditionally been addressed through negotiations, with countries seeking greater market access for their goods and services.
However, she noted that tariffs are increasingly being used as a tool to tackle trade imbalances.
“Now the imbalance is being sought to be addressed through other means, where, as you rightly said, tariffs have become weaponised. Tariff was an instrument of negotiation, and tariff had a certain framework within which you would apply it. Today, the framework is there, but tariffs are going,” she said.
Sitharaman also questioned whether India could adopt a similar approach in its trade relationship with China, given the sharp rise in the bilateral trade deficit.
“The trade imbalance with China for India, for instance, since 2014, has been growing exponentially. So, when you’re talking of trade and trade imbalance being the sole criteria to reduce the imbalance, to what extent beyond negotiation can you go?” she asked.
Her comments come after US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said last week that the US and India were working towards finalising a bilateral trade agreement, but that a deal was not imminent.
Greer indicated that US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi could hold another phone call “very soon” to assess progress in the negotiations.
Speaking at a press conference following the G20 Trade Ministers’ Meeting in Milwaukee, Greer said the two sides had identified the remaining areas of disagreement and were working towards an agreement.
“We had a very constructive conversation, Minister Goyal and myself. Our staff is meeting right now since they’re in the country, and we’re here,” Greer said.
Greer had met Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers’ Meeting on September 30, where the two held a “productive discussion” on the early conclusion of a mutually beneficial interim trade agreement.
On the India-EU trade deal, Sitharaman described the agreement as a significant example of India’s approach to negotiating and concluding trade pacts.
She said calling it the “Mother of all deals” was appropriate, given that it would cover an economic bloc representing around two billion people and encompass a substantial share of global trade and GDP.
“Ultimately, you’re tailoring the agreement to keep national interest alive but to survive in a very challenging global environment where no WTO-related laws have been left to be respected,” Sitharaman said, adding that countries had increasingly moved away from adhering to established rules.

articles.title: India-US trade talks hit a plateau, says Sitharaman - Livemint
articles.summary: India-US trade talks hit a plateau, says Sitharaman  Livemint
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: India-US trade negotiations have reached a “plateau” as both sides find it increasingly difficult to make further concessions, even as a trade agreement remains to be finalized, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday.
Speaking at the Munich Leaders’ Meeting in New Delhi, Sitharaman said the negotiations had been “hard and very rigorously negotiated” and remained ongoing, but that further movement could prove difficult.
“The US agreement, which is yet to be finalized, has been a hard and very rigorously negotiated agreement. The agreement’s negotiations are still ongoing, although we’d like to believe that both sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult. But maybe, if there are rooms to operate from, both sides would do it,” the finance minister said.
Sitharaman said the two sides were approaching the negotiations from different positions because of the trade imbalance between them, with the US seeking to narrow its deficit with India.
“What is the predominant feature of the trade relations between India and the US? The trade balance is very much in our favour. Naturally, the deficit is there on their side, or the balance is going unfavourably for the US. So, they would want to reduce that imbalance, and their desire would be to see, as much as possible, get some kind of, from their point of view, making up for all that they’ve lost over these years,” she said.
Bilateral trade between India and the US rose to $140.77 billion in fiscal year 2026 (FY26) from $132.14 billion in FY25, according to data from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT). India’s exports to the US edged up to $87.31 billion from $86.51 billion, while imports rose to $53.45 billion from $45.63 billion. As a result, India’s trade surplus with the US narrowed to $33.86 billion from $40.89 billion.
India and the US began negotiations for a bilateral trade agreement in February 2025, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Donald Trump formally announced the talks.
She said this also illustrated why India could not apply a single template to all its trade negotiations.
“From our side, in a way and I’m not comparing at all, but I want to put that before this learned audience as such, templates can exist for different countries in different parts of the world. If that principle of trade imbalance, which has to be reduced for them to consider anything more, I would think that is the way in which the US would look at China, or India would look at China.”
Sitharaman said trade relationships with different partners have different structures and negotiating priorities.
She said trade negotiations between India and the European Union (EU) had to account for sensitive sectors on both sides, including agriculture, dairy, meat, and soybean. The talks also had to address supply-chain resilience, including the need to find new partners where existing supply chains have already been disrupted.
The contrast with China is sharper. The minister said India’s trade deficit with China has grown sharply since 2014 and that countries are increasingly seeking to address trade imbalances through means other than traditional negotiations, with tariffs becoming “weaponized” in the process.
India cannot simply replicate such approaches with China and would instead have to rely on negotiation and give-and-take, she said.
The comments underscore how India is negotiating multiple trade arrangements at a time when tariff concessions are only one part of the equation. Supply-chain resilience, strategic autonomy and geopolitical risks are increasingly shaping the terms of trade policy.
Sitharaman also argued that bilateral and multilateral trade arrangements have never been mutually exclusive. But the balance has shifted towards bilateral agreements as institutions meant to guide and regulate the multilateral system have weakened.
“Multilateralism is not going to go away, and multilateralism shouldn’t go away,” Sitharaman said, while adding that the weakening of institutions such as the WTO has made countries more confident about pursuing bilateral arrangements.
The remarks come as India works simultaneously on trade arrangements with several partners, including the US and Canada.
The Munich Leaders Meetings are part of the Munich Security Conference (MSC), established in 1963 for high-level security dialogue. The 4–5 October New Delhi meeting, in cooperation with the Indian government, has focused on economic security, resilient supply chains, strategic autonomy and the changing role of emerging and middle powers.
Sitharaman said India is also moving towards a new template for bilateral investment protection agreements. The framework, incorporating lessons from recent agreements with countries including the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Saudi Arabia, is expected to receive cabinet approval shortly.
Mint reported on 25 September that the Union cabinet would shortly consider overhauling the decade-old bilateral investment treaty (BIT) template to make it easier for foreign companies to seek international arbitration over investment disputes in India.
Negotiations are already underway with Canada and several other countries based on elements of the proposed framework, Sitharaman said. India hopes to conclude bilateral investment protection agreements with at least three more countries by December, while a pact with Canada could be concluded by December or early next year if negotiations progress as planned.
The broader message from the discussion was that India is increasingly viewing trade policy through the lens of economic security. European participants at the meeting similarly argued that India and Europe have a shared interest in diversifying supply chains, reducing external dependencies and building strategic autonomy.

The 29-year-old pilot, identified as Hamam al-Hammami, joined flydubai in February as the airline was rapidly rebuilding its workforce after the pandemic. The recruitment of the pilot has now come under scrutiny following the attempted crash.
Flydubai has built its network around destinations that some Western carriers have avoided because of security or operational challenges. NEW DELHI: The Cabinet on Tuesday approved setting up India’s first integrated transport and logistics authority, giving the new body a mandate to plan, appraise and monitor projects worth over Rs 500 crore across roads, railways, ports, aviation, waterways, urban mobility and logistics.
The Integrated Transport and Logistics Authority (ITLA) is aimed at ending fragmented planning across multiple transport ministries and agencies and driving greater coordination and multi-modal integration in infrastructure development. Announcing the decision, I&B minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said, “By fostering greater coordination and multi-modal integration, ITLA is a new institution responsible for prospective planning for infrastructure development in the country.”
The new agency is modelled on similar institutions in the US, UK, Germany, Australia and Japan, and was first reported by TOI in April 2024.
Govt said ITLA will also create a unified transport data repository by obtaining relevant transport and logistics datasets from multiple sources, including GSTN e-way bills, FASTag, Vahan, GPS-based systems, urban traffic management systems and other databases. It will undertake data analytics for planning, monitoring and impact assessment.

articles.title: From building mobile technology to backing startups: Samartha Nagabhushanam’s marks his three-decade journey - India.com
articles.summary: From building mobile technology to backing startups: Samartha Nagabhushanam’s marks his three-decade journey  India.com
articles.full_text:
Bengaluru: From working on telecommunications technology in the 1990s to building mobile handset businesses and subsequently mentoring startups, technology executive and entrepreneur Dr. Samartha Nagabhushanam has spent more than three decades across different phases of India’s evolving technology ecosystem.
An electronics and communication engineering graduate, Nagabhushanam began his professional career in 1993. His early assignments included roles in electronics and telecommunications before he moved to Hughes Software Systems and later Silicon Automation Systems, now known as Sasken Communication Technologies. His work during this period largely revolved around telecommunications protocols and emerging mobile technologies.
A significant phase of his career began in 2003 when Japanese electronics company Kyocera established Kyocera Wireless India in Bengaluru. Nagabhushanam headed the initial engineering team and was subsequently appointed Managing Director of the Indian operation in 2004.
Under his leadership, the Bengaluru centre expanded its work in CDMA handset development. By 2006, the operation had grown to around 550 employees and was working towards end-to-end handset development for international markets. The centre was also involved in developing devices for India, including Kyocera’s K122 low-cost handset.
In 2009, MindTree acquired Kyocera Wireless India and used the business to establish its handset division, N!Mo, or Next in Mobility. Nagabhushanam took charge of the business as President and CEO. The division worked on ready-to-brand mobile devices, including an Android smartphone.
After his corporate technology career, Nagabhushanam moved increasingly towards entrepreneurship. He founded Aseema Softnet Technologies, later renamed FiDZeal, focusing on Android device engineering. In 2015, he joined 5BARz International’s India operations as CEO and also served as the company’s global Chief Operating Officer. The business worked on technology aimed at improving indoor cellular connectivity.
His entrepreneurial interests have since expanded into advertising technology, Web3, startup incubation and digital engagement. He co-founded Eleos Social and its Indian technology arm CuberaTech, which works on AI-driven advertising technology. The company has developed platforms covering programmatic advertising, attribution, exchanges and audience discovery.
Nagabhushanam is also a co-founder of Cirus Foundation and Ramaiah Evolute, a not-for-profit startup accelerator associated with the Ramaiah Group of Institutions. Through Ramaiah Evolute, he has been involved in mentoring and supporting early-stage entrepreneurs while advocating greater access to capital, networks and business guidance for emerging founders.
More recently, he has been associated with Star Fandom, which launched an AI-enabled fan engagement application dedicated to late Kannada actor Puneeth Rajkumar in 2025.
Alongside his business roles, Nagabhushanam has spoken at educational institutions and technology forums on entrepreneurship, innovation and emerging technologies. His recent writing has explored areas including deep technology, artificial intelligence in advertising, online gaming regulation and approaches to responsible business growth.
In 2023, Tumkur University conferred a Doctor of Letters (D.Litt.) on Nagabhushanam for his work examining the leadership styles of chief executives who built large organisations.
As India’s technology landscape moves from traditional telecommunications and mobile engineering towards AI-led platforms and startup-driven innovation, Nagabhushanam’s career reflects several of the shifts the country’s technology sector has undergone over the past three decades.

New Delhi: India’s production of finished steel increased by 3.7 per cent to 81.8 million tonnes during the first half of the current financial year (April-September), compared with the corresponding figure of 78.8 million tonnes in the same period last year, according to data released by the Ministry of Steel on Tuesday.
The country’s consumption of finished steel shot up by a robust 7.9 per cent to 84.9 million tonnes during the first half (H1) of 2026-27 from 79 million tonnes in the same period of the last financial year, as demand from big ticket infrastructure projects taken up by the government in the highways, railways and port sectors fuelled demand.
India’s steel exports also surged by 26.2 per cent during the first half of the current financial year to 3.55 million tonnes compared with the corresponding figure of 2.81 million tonnes in April-Sept of the previous financial year.
In value terms, the exports during April-September jumped by 28.9 per cent to Rs 28,263.7 crore from Rs 21,931.5 crore in the same period last year.
The country’s production of crude steel was recorded at 85.1 million tonnes in April-September of the current financial year, compared with 82.7 million tonnes in the same period of the previous year, which represents a 2.9 per cent increase.
India’s total crude steelmaking capacity currently stands at 222.9 million tonnes per annum, keeping the industry on track to achieve the National Steel Policy target of 300 million tonnes per annum by 2030, according to an official statement.
Meanwhile, mining giant NMDC’s iron ore production rose 8 per cent year-on-year to 4.04 million tonnes in September 2026, taking the H1 FY 2026–27 output to 27.3 million tonnes, up nearly 23 per cent over H1 FY 2025–26 — keeping the company on track towards its annual production targets, the statement said.
NMDC has commissioned its 2 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) pellet plant at Nagarnar, Chhattisgarh, completing its Rs 5,427-crore integrated project. The project comprises an iron ore processing plant at Bacheli, a 135-km, 15 MTPA slurry pipeline and the Nagarnar pellet plant, which uses Straight Grate Induration technology. It will enable value addition from Bailadila iron ore fines and slimes, reduce road transport of ore and strengthen NMDC’s presence across the iron ore value chain.
The Ministry of Steel has decided to set up a Steel Industry Safety Council (SISC), an apex body chaired by the Secretary, Ministry of Steel, to strengthen safety standards, accident prevention and safety culture across the steel industry.

articles.title: Assam river port comes alive after 70 years as methanol-laden barge sails for Dhaka - The New Indian Express
articles.summary: Assam river port comes alive after 70 years as methanol-laden barge sails for Dhaka  The New Indian Express
articles.full_text:
GUWAHATI: A barge carrying 540 metric tons of methanol left the Bogibeel terminal in Dibrugarh for Dhaka in Bangladesh on Monday, marking the first such international voyage from this upper Assam town since 1956.
Union Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal flagged off the vessel DLB Patkai. Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma joined the ceremony virtually.
The methanol, produced by state-owned Assam Petro-Chemicals Ltd. at Namrup, is bound for Pangaon Port in Dhaka. The vessel will travel about 768 km down National Waterway-2 on the Brahmaputra River in India to the India-Bangladesh border and then, continue along the Indo-Bangladesh Protocol Route, covering a total distance of 1,300 km.
The voyage is being observed as a test of whether the Brahmaputra can serve as a commercially viable freight corridor linking the Northeast to overseas markets. The shipment became possible after customs and immigration complexes were set up at Bogibeel and Dhubri recently.
“Our grandparents grew up hearing the steamer whistle at Dibrugarh Ghat. For 70 years, that whistle fell silent and the ships stopped coming. Today, a ship leaves Dibrugarh for the world again. The river never failed us. What it lacked for decades was the will to revive it,” Sonowal said.
He asked the youth of Assam to dream with this river. He said under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Dibrugarh, the Tea Capital of India, was reclaiming its past glory as a great river port.
“We are building it with world-class infrastructure while honouring its heritage," he further said.
Sarma called it a proud day for Assam. “Assam’s own product is now traveling to an international market on Assam’s own river. The Northeast is no longer a frontier. It is India's gateway to the East,” the Chief Minister said.
Dibrugarh was once among the busiest river ports in eastern India. Government steamers reached the town from Calcutta, now Kolkata, by 1856. In 1882, the Dibru-Sadiya Railway began operating from the Dibrugarh steamer ghat. By 1913, steamers sailed up the Brahmaputra to the town daily, carrying tea, timber and passengers.
The 1947 partition cut that route, forcing Assam’s goods to pass through East Pakistan to reach Calcutta. A 1950 earthquake disturbed the riverbed at Dibrugarh. Regular bookings from Dibrugarh Ghat stopped in 1954, and the ghat closed on October 15, 1956, as tea shipments shifted to rail.
The 1965 war between India and Pakistan suspended cross-border river trade. India and Bangladesh signed a river trade protocol in 1972. In 1988, the 891-km stretch of river Brahmaputra from Sadiya to Dhubri was declared National Waterway-2. Regular cargo service on the waterway did not begin until December 2017, when cement moved from Pandu in Guwahati to lower Assam’s Dhubri.

Iran's military said on Monday it retained full control over the Strait of Hormuz despite changes in US tactics, as the rial fell to record lows, the oil minister resigned and Washington claimed Tehran had not exported a single barrel of crude in September.
"All movements (in Hormuz) are under the control of the armed forces of the Islamic Republic," Brigadier General Aziz Jafari, commander of Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Joint Air Defence Headquarters, said Monday.
Hours before Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad's resignation was announced, he said in a video released by Iranian media that revenue from oil already sold would be collected and the process would continue.

Pezeshkian had acknowledged in August that the blockade was disrupting exports. "We used to sell oil; now we cannot sell it," he said. The new acting oil minister pledged to maximise production and continue exports through new strategies.
Ship-tracking company Kpler recorded crude exports from the region excluding Iran at between 19.5 and 22.5 million barrels per day in the final week of September, above the pre-war regional average of 18 million barrels per day.
The euro broke through 300,000 tomans on Iran's informal market, while the US dollar hit a record 270,000 tomans — more than double its level at the start of this year, when it stood at around 135,000 tomans.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told foreign ambassadors in Tehran that the conflict had no military solution. "If our enemies once again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be firmer than before," he said.
"Only negotiations founded on justice and fairness can offer a way to end this conflict." He said the Strait could be fully reopened and shipping restored within seven days if Tehran's conditions were met and hostile measures lifted.
Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Iran had received proposals from Washington through intermediaries but would not accept one-sided demands.
"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and definitive, and until our seven conditions based on the Islamabad memorandum are met, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened," Ghalibaf said.

TOI correspondant from Washington:
 In Montana, ‘traffic’ is when you have to wait for three deer and a stray cow to cross the highway, so goes the joke about a state where “just down the road” can mean a two-hour drive with no cellphone service. Yet for Montana Governor Greg Gianforte, one road this week stretches 8,000 miles, from the Big Sky State to India, home to 1.4 billion potential customers.
Gianforte, a Republican, arrived in New Delhi on Monday at the head of a delegation of more than 30 Montanans representing agriculture, higher education, critical minerals, manufacturing, photonics, quantum technology and bioscience. The mission runs through October 9 and continues to Sri Lanka, and its major commercial pitch is deliciously simple: buy our daal, dahlings.
Montana is America's largest producer of lentils and chickpeas and India is the world's largest consumer and importer of pulse crops. In 2025, however, India's purchases of Montana peas, lentils and chickpeas were for chicken feed, only about $14 million, which, along with commercial aircraft parts, made India Montana's 29th-largest trading partner.
For a state of just over a million people – the population of an Indian mofussil town – India represents a huge opportunity. 
Montana's agricultural economy is substantial, but its producers need markets far beyond the state's borders, and indeed beyond the US and that is precisely where Gianforte's India trip collides with the conflict in Republican politics: the same MAGA constituency demanding that America buy American is also deeply suspicious when American governors go abroad to sell American products, particularly when the prospective customers are Indians.
The backlash in this case has been instant and fierce. MAGA hardliners have questioned why Montana should deepen ties with India when, they argue, Indian students and faculty are "capturing" Montana universities.
One viral discussion singled out Montana State University faculty with Indian roots, including Shivali Banerjee, an agricultural engineering professor with a PhD from IIT Bombay, and Sreekala and Dilpreet Bajwa, senior figures in the university's agriculture and engineering programs. Montana State's own records identify Sreekala Bajwa as vice president for agriculture and Dilpreet Bajwa as head of mechanical and industrial engineering.
The irony is difficult to miss: Montana wants to sell agricultural products to India while some of its political activists are objecting to Indians teaching Montanans how to improve agriculture and engineering. "You need to be in America working for Americans, not jews or Indians. You are a traitor to the US,” one post aimed at Gianforte read.
The controversy illustrates a growing bind for Republican governors, with Texas governor Greg Abbott facing a similar backlash in recent weeks. Their job is not to conduct immigration policy; it is to grow their states' economies. They want foreign investment, export markets, international students, researchers, and skilled workers, provided all of this produces jobs, tax revenue and prosperity at home. But the political language of the MAGA movement increasingly questions the efficacy of this model.
Abbott, whose state has a bigger economy and larger Indian-origin population, has simultaneously cultivated Texas's enormous desi business community and taken a harder line on H-1B visas.
In January, he ordered Texas state agencies and universities to freeze new H-1B petitions, arguing that jobs should go first to Texans. Yet he and other Texas Republicans are also aggressively courting Indian-American voters and business interests, creating an obvious tension between economic pragmatism and anti-immigration rhetoric from the MAGA base.
Gianforte's dilemma is even more excruciating. Montana needs buyers; its farmers cannot sell lentils merely to Montanans, and its universities cannot become globally competitive by hiring only people born within state lines.
And its emerging technology and scientific sectors cannot prosper by pretending talent stops at the adjoining Canadian border.
There is a lesson for Gianforte from Montana’s own diplomatic history. Mike Mansfield, the state’s legendary senator and later ambassador to Japan, was a strong proponent in the 1960s of good ties with India.
He was among the first lawmakers to appreciate India’s desire for strategic autonomy, and he understood that being from a small state should not inhibit big thinking. The foreign relations titan looked across the Pacific when much of America was looking inward, helping deepen US engagement with Asia, including India.
Gianforte’s mission is more prosaic, selling Montana lentils, peas and chickpeas to India’s 1.4 billion people — but the principle is much the same: Big Sky country cannot afford small-world thinking.
