articles.title: Pakistan needs political stability — but how? - Pakistan Observer
articles.summary: Pakistan needs political stability — but how?  Pakistan Observer
articles.full_text:
PAKISTAN desperately needs political stability. Economic recovery, investment, employment, exports and long-term development all require a political environment in which policies are predictable and institutions can function without continuous disruption. But the real question is: how can Pakistan achieve political stability? Political stability should not be confused with keeping one political party or government in power. Nor does it mean suppressing political disagreement. In a democracy, governments can change and opposition parties can challenge those in power. What must remain stable are the constitutional rules, institutions and basic direction of the state.
Pakistan’s fundamental problem is that political competition too often becomes a struggle for control of the entire state. When governments change, policies change, institutions are politicized and accountability processes become controversial. The result is uncertainty for citizens, businesses and investors. The country therefore needs a new political understanding — a Charter of Political Stability. The major political parties should agree on a minimum set of democratic rules. Governments should complete their constitutional terms unless removed through constitutional procedures. Opposition parties should have the right to criticize and challenge those in power. Elections should be conducted through credible and transparent processes, while disputes should be settled through institutions rather than confrontation in the streets.
Winning an election should not give a government unlimited authority, while losing an election should not justify attempts to destabilize the constitutional system. Pakistan needs a culture in which governments may change without the system collapsing every time they do. No political system can remain stable when a substantial section of society does not trust the electoral process. The Election Commission and other institutions responsible for elections must therefore command public confidence. Electoral disputes should be resolved quickly, transparently and through established legal mechanisms. The objective should not be to guarantee victory for any particular party, but to ensure that the voters’ mandate is respected, whatever the result.
Pakistan’s political system also needs stronger parliamentary institutions. Major national policies should be debated in Parliament rather than determined through informal arrangements or executive decisions alone. Parliament must become the principal forum for debating taxation, economic reforms, constitutional changes and national priorities. Political parties themselves must strengthen their parliamentary culture. Democracy cannot become institutionalized if political parties remain heavily dependent on personalities and families. Internal democracy, transparent party finances, merit-based candidate selection and greater participation by younger people and professionals could gradually transform them into stronger institutions.
Constitutional institutions must respect their roles: Political stability also requires clarity about institutional boundaries. The military has an important constitutional role in national defence and security, while elected governments are responsible for political governance. The judiciary has its constitutional responsibilities, as do Parliament and the executive. Pakistan needs an institutional equilibrium in which no institution attempts to permanently substitute itself for another. This is not merely a political principle; it is also an economic necessity. Investors and businesses need confidence that policies will be determined through predictable constitutional processes rather than changing according to political circumstances.
Rule of law must be non-negotiable: There can be no durable political stability without the rule of law. If citizens believe that laws apply differently to the powerful and the powerless, confidence in the entire system declines. Accountability must therefore be independent, transparent and consistent. It should not be perceived as an instrument for punishing political opponents or protecting political allies. The principle should be simple: those who hold power must be accountable, but accountability itself must operate according to law. One of Pakistan’s biggest weaknesses is the lack of continuity in economic policy.
Pakistan needs a 10- to 15-year national economic framework agreed upon by the major political forces.
Tax reform, exports, energy, agriculture, industrialization, investment, education and human development should not become partisan issues.
Governments should remain free to modify individual policies, but the country’s fundamental economic direction should remain broadly consistent.
Political stability is also affected by economic inequality.
When ordinary citizens face heavy taxation while powerful groups receive exemptions and concessions, people naturally question the fairness of the system.
Pakistan needs a taxation system that is broad-based, transparent and equitable.
The burden should not continually fall on documented middle- and lower-income groups while influential segments remain protected through exemptions, concessions or weak enforcement.
Economic fairness can strengthen political legitimacy.
Political stability also requires the state to address long-term demographic pressures.
Rapid population growth places additional pressure on education, health, employment, housing, food, water and public finances.
Population policy should therefore become part of national planning rather than remaining an issue that successive governments avoid.
Ultimately, Pakistan needs something deeper than another political compromise between individuals or parties.
It needs a new political social contract based on five principles: Constitutional supremacy, credible elections, rule of law, respect for institutional boundaries, continuity of economic policy.

Under such an arrangement, political parties would compete vigorously for power within agreed constitutional boundaries. The opposition would seek to replace the government through elections, not institutional disruption. The government would respect the opposition’s constitutional role rather than treating criticism as an existential threat. State institutions would perform their constitutional responsibilities without becoming instruments of political instability. Pakistan should not seek political stability simply for the sake of stability. The purpose is much bigger: to create an environment in which the economy can grow, businesses can invest, institutions can function, young people can find employment and citizens can trust the state.
Political stability alone will not solve Pakistan’s problems. But without it, economic and governance reforms will remain vulnerable to reversal. Pakistan’s crisis therefore demands two changes simultaneously: economic reform and political reform. country cannot permanently repair its economy while its political system remains unpredictable. Nor can it build a stable political order while economic inequality, weak governance, institutional conflict and lack of rule of law continue. The real challenge is not simply to change governments. It is to change the rules of the game so that governments can change without destabilizing Pakistan. That is the political stability Pakistan urgently needs.
—The writer is Senior Retd bureaucrat, based in Lahore.

articles.title: 'Islam wanting to take over': Donald Trump reacts to France school protests - The Times of India
articles.summary: 'Islam wanting to take over': Donald Trump reacts to France school protests  The Times of India"Islam Wanting To Take Over": Trump On Mass Student Protests In France  NDTVTrump blames France unrest on Islam, migration  The New Indian ExpressFrench foreign minister responds to Trump over student protests  Anadolu AjansıTrump rips French riots as possible troop shifts in Western Europe looms  The Center Square
articles.full_text:
US President 
Donald Trump
 on Wednesday reacted to growing student protests in France, claiming the demonstrations reflected “mass migration” and saying they were about “Islam wanting to take over” the country.
“What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
More than 266,000 people took part in nationwide demonstrations on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, according to France’s Interior Ministry. The protests, which began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September, have spread across the country as students demand more funding for education.
Police fired tear gas and clashed with small groups of protesters in Paris after an otherwise largely peaceful march. Nearly 500 people were detained, the ministry said.
Students have been blockading schools and boycotting classes for more than two weeks. Police have made more than 6,500 arrests since the protests began, most involving minors, according to officials.
The use of tear gas, batons and other riot-control weapons against teenagers has drawn criticism from students, parents and teachers. 
Some student groups have called for further protests on Thursday.
French interior minister Laurent Nuñez defended the police response, saying it had been proportionate in “almost all cases” and that officers had intervened when protests turned violent.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school authorities needed to listen to students and address their concerns. He also condemned what he called “ultra violence” around schools and rejected allegations of racism in the police response as a “lie”.
The protests have become an early flashpoint in France’s presidential election campaign, amid wider anger over public spending, poverty and wealth inequality. Rising fuel prices linked to the Iran war have added to the discontent.
Felix Barney, a university student, criticised the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn't make “any sense to hit minors.”
The latest tensions also come after a 15-year-old boy lost a hand in an incident involving a police stun grenade on Monday. Nuñez said 715 police officers had been injured during the unrest.

articles.title: Indian opposition lawmakers detained during protest against poll chief - Dawn
articles.summary: Indian opposition lawmakers detained during protest against poll chief  Dawn
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: Indian police detained several opposition lawmakers in the capital New Delhi on Tuesday for trying to breach barricades during a protest march to demand the resignation of the election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.
The march presents a fresh political challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar protests forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.
Parties opposing Modi’s government along with members of the popular ‘cockroach’ youth movement protested against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar after the Indian Express newspaper reported divisions in the poll body last month.
The reported differences over the lists and voter registration procedures stoked concern about the neutrality of the commission, led by a Modi appointee.
“The election commission is a puppet in the hands of the government,” Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge told reporters as the march began. “We are fighting to save our democracy.”
Lawmakers carried placards, waved the national flag, and shouted slogans against Kumar during the march, roughly 1km-long, or less than a mile, to the Election Commission headquarters from parliament, through the centre of Delhi.
Some carried placards calling Kumar a traitor and accused the BJP of snatching away the right to vote, while they sat on the road outside the panel’s office, demanding to meet him.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka and several more stood on police barricades there, waving the national flag and calling for Kumar to resign.
Hundreds of security personnel, some wearing riot gear and carrying batons, tried to stop Gandhi and others from entering the election commission.
“After failing multiple times, Congress leaders have decided to establish anarchy in the country and attack institutions,” BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra told reporters before Tuesday’s protest.
TV channels said the Gandhi siblings were among those briefly detained before being released. The duo sought entry through the grounds of the state radio office next door, where they sat in protest under a tree after the route was blocked, the channels said.

articles.summary: Sri Lanka’s Economic and Geopolitical Balancing Act  Carnegie Endowment for International Peace
articles.full_text:
One year after a historic election, Sri Lanka’s new left-leaning government faces mounting pressure to translate its reform promises into action.
Sri Lanka’s Economic and Geopolitical Balancing Act
Economic recovery has brought Sri Lanka a modicum of stability, but domestic strains and great-power rivalry could test how long it lasts.
Introduction
On March 4, 2026, Sri Lanka was caught off-guard when the U.S. Navy submarine, the USS Charlotte, sank the Iranian frigate, IRIS Dena, 19 nautical miles off Sri Lanka’s southwest Galle coast. The attack left 104 crew members dead and brought the 2026 Iran war into subcontinental waters. The Sri Lanka Navy rescued thirty-two Iranian sailors, but the Sri Lankan government’s overall response drew criticism from opposition leaders.
President Anura Kumara Dissanayake—head of the National People’s Power coalition, which is led by the Marxist-Leninist party, the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP)—clarified to the Sri Lankan parliament: “Our unwavering stance on this matter is one of neutrality.” But the opposition leader, Sajith Premadasa of the United National Party, challenged Dissanayake’s neutrality position as an excuse for passivity. The incident was “a death blow to Sri Lanka’s sovereignty,” Premadasa claimed as he pressed the president to condemn American and Israeli aggression against Iran as well as Iran’s targeting of other Gulf states. Former foreign minister G. L. Peiris was blunter: the “Sri Lankan government has actually insulted Iran, which is a friendly nation where Sri Lanka is concerned.” The opposition also questioned the government’s failure to act quickly on the Iranian frigate’s request to enter Sri Lankan territorial waters and its apparent lack of awareness of the USS Charlotte’s movements.
Dissanayake’s foreign policy of neutrality offers Colombo room to focus on economic recovery, but, as the IRIS Dena incident shows, international economic and geopolitical turbulence will test how long that posture can be sustained. The country’s 2024 presidential elections offered much-needed political clarity after an acute economic crisis in 2022, the ouster of Sri Lanka’s president Gotabaya Rajapaksa amid the Aragalaya (Struggle) protests, and two years of political uncertainty. The NPP’s promise of reforms and the continuation of an International Monetary Fund (IMF) bailout have been key to Sri Lanka’s post-2022 social contract.
Yet with the current IMF loan cycle ending in 2027 and national elections due in 2029, early signs of volatility in Sri Lanka’s domestic and international politics are beginning to show. At home, the NPP’s inability to deliver many of its promised reforms signals that even if a 2022-style meltdown is unlikely, the economy remains under pressure. Unlike in 2022, however, a future crisis could strengthen a coercive left-wing one-party state rather than produce another popular uprising that sweeps a government from power. With regard to the country’s external relations, reliance on IMF funding—supported by an Indian backstop—has drawn Sri Lanka closer to India and the West. However, Chinese capital and finance, not just for infrastructure development but also through illicit networks, are also shaping Sri Lanka’s domestic and international politics. Looking to the future, Dissanayake’s principal challenge is to preserve the political and economic stability that his government has consolidated after 2024 while simultaneously managing multiple pressures that could unsettle both the NPP’s domestic moderation and its carefully calibrated foreign policy.

Understand the world with the latest from our scholars around the world.
Domestic Politics and the Limits of Reform
Sri Lanka turned a corner in September 2024 when the NPP coalition trounced traditional political parties and went on to win 159 of 225 parliamentary seats. The elections marked the start of a new political and economic journey for a country that had witnessed acute turmoil from 2022 to 2024. Dissanayake promised to use his electoral mandate to reform Sri Lanka’s economic and political structures to prevent a recurrence of a similar economic crisis. Yet beyond adhering to the IMF’s terms and conditions and tightening some anti-corruption regulations, much of the government’s broader reform agenda remains stalled. Three primary factors offer insight into the cause and consequences of this subpar performance: the risks associated with implementing reforms, tension between the JVP’s organizational nature and political character, and sensitive civil-military relations.
A Stalled Reform Agenda
In the run-up to the 2024 elections, Dissanayake promised to implement a series of reforms if the NPP was brought to power. These included combating corruption, reforming government institutions and the economy, improving living conditions, overhauling the taxation system, repealing the controversial Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) and the Online Safety Act, establishing independent prosecution and accountability mechanisms, and, most significantly, abolishing the executive presidency and its concentration of political power. These promises were made against the backdrop of a May 2023 IMF bailout that was negotiated by former president Ranil Wickremesinghe. Dissanayake agreed to continue with the loan agreement and meet its terms rather than seek to renegotiate it as the NPP had promised during the election campaign.
Of these promised reforms, Colombo has made the greatest progress in complying with IMF requirements and pursuing modest anti-corruption measures. Thanks to the IMF program and political stability since 2024, the Sri Lankan economy surpassed expectations, recording a 5 percent growth in its GDP in 2024. Its foreign exchange reserves stood at $6.5 billion in June 2026 despite nearly a 10 percent decline in tourism due to the Iran war. This relative stability has persisted despite limited foreign investment, which stood at $1.04 billion in 2025, of which $352 million is in equity and $692 million is in the form of debt instruments. Anti-corruption measures—such as the Proceeds of Crime Act (2025) to recover assets, a stronger asset declaration system, mandatory reporting of audit-detected corruption, and proactive enforcement—have also helped fuel Sri Lanka’s overall economic rebound.
But economic recovery and political consolidation have not led to delivery on other promised reforms. Though Dissanayake did abolish state-funded privileges for former presidents, he has failed to eliminate the executive presidency or repeal draconian security laws. In December 2025, Dissanayake’s Cabinet proposed the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill to replace the PTA. (A supplementary gazette to this bill was presented in September 2026.) This bill is yet to pass the parliament, and it has kept intact several draconian PTA measures, such as prolonged pre-charge and pre-trial detention, as well as unchecked executive power to proscribe individuals and organizations without judicial oversight. Plans to overhaul the taxation system—admittedly a complex, technical, and time-consuming issue—and strengthen judicial independence remain confined within opaque committees with limited signs of visible progress. This raises the question of why a party with such a large mandate and economic stability has not moved more swiftly to deliver on its campaign promises.
There are two compelling reasons for the slow pace of reforms. First, sequencing matters. Delaying certain economic measures allows Dissanayake to postpone the changes until the country formally meets IMF requirements. Additionally, as long as the economy remains stable, there is little public political pressure to initiate large-scale reforms. As the end of the current IMF program approaches in 2027, Colombo will focus its administrative energies on renegotiating the terms to secure more support. Against this backdrop, it makes little sense to launch sweeping taxation and judicial reforms while existential financial negotiations are ongoing. This is especially true if there is no clear political cost to be paid for inaction, given the dismal state of the opposition parties. The outcome of Dissanayake’s negotiations with the IMF, along with the JVP’s political standing in 2027–2028, will determine the government’s appetite for reform.
The second reason the JVP has failed to push reforms is more politically straightforward. The existence of the executive presidency was a significant grievance for the JVP when it was the opposition, but the party enjoys the position’s outsized authority now that it holds the reins of power. Dissanayake is experiencing a rare moment wherein a Sinhala-dominated Marxist-Leninist party has come to power in Sri Lanka through the ballot box. The fact that it enjoys electoral support in the Tamil-dominated north and east as much as in the Sinhala-dominated south and central Sri Lanka is a testament to its appeal as an alternative to the traditional, family-based parties plagued by years of anti-incumbency. The JVP has little incentive to dilute the most powerful executive instrument to deliver on promises midway through its tenure, even if doing so was a core manifesto promise.
The JVP: Marxist-Leninist Core, Social Democratic Face
The NPP is a coalition of nearly twenty founding constituents that range from labor unions and collectives to the Sri Lanka Communist Party–Alternative Group. The JVP is the organizational and political core of this coalition, despite being a small cadre-based party with a history of anti-state militant activism during the 1970s and 1980s. It rose to power with an unexpectedly large mandate and knit together a coalition of multiple constituent parties, the latter of which has generated an underappreciated pressure to govern with caution and conservatism without rocking the proverbial boat. Karnataka is repositioning its global innovation engagement from event-led interactions to sustained partnerships, with the State preparing to roll out a new engagement framework and a dedicated physical platform for international innovation collaborations, Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, IT & Bt and e-Governance, Government of Karnataka, said on October 6, 2026 in Bengaluru.
Speaking at the Global Innovation Alliance (GIA) Meet, organised by the Department of Electronics, IT, Biotechnology and S&T ahead of the Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) 2026, Kharge highlighted the need to convert Karnataka’s international partnerships into tangible opportunities for startups, companies, institutions and investors.

A key component of the next phase is GIGA – Global Innovation and Growth Alliance, a proposed permanent physical infrastructure in Bengaluru that will provide international startups, innovation agencies, delegations and institutions with workspace, meeting and programme facilities. It is intended to connect international partners with Karnataka’s Centres of Excellence, incubators, universities, industry and investors.
The initiative signals a shift towards creating a more permanent landing platform for international companies and innovation organisations seeking to establish partnerships and explore opportunities in Karnataka.
The GIA network, launched in 2017 under the Karnataka Unit for International Co-operation, has grown from 10 partner countries in 2018 to more than 40 countries in 2026.

US Begins Largest Denaturalisation Drive, Targets 40 Including Indian
Justice Department seeks citizenship revocation over alleged fraud, serious offences and misrepresentation
The US launched the largest denaturalisation effort in modern history by moving to strip 40 individuals, including one of Indian origin, of their American citizenship, the Department of Justice said.The 40 individuals facing denaturalisation actions in multiple US courts have been accused of serious offences, including acting as an agent for a foreign government, committing voluntary manslaughter, and aggravated sodomy against a special-needs man.
Balwinder Singh of California is facing denaturalisation action in the state's Eastern District court for using a fraudulent identity to gain admission to and acquire a US citizenship. "Today's announcement marks the largest denaturalisation effort in modern history," said Attorney General Todd Blanche on Monday.
Under the Immigration and Nationality Act, a naturalised US citizen's citizenship may be revoked and certificate of naturalisation cancelled, if it was procured illegally or by concealment of a material fact or by willful misrepresentation.
"Every single one of these individuals lied their way into US citizenship," said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department's Civil Division.
"This administration will continue to pursue the largest denaturalisation effort in department history to restore trust and integrity in US citizenship. Our message is clear: the United States will not tolerate deception in the naturalisation process," Shumate said.
According to the Department of Justice, Singh, in 1992,  submitted an immigration application under the identity of Balwinder Singh. In 2003, he sought and received permanent resident status under a second identity.
"Fingerprints establish that Singh submitted both applications. In 2009, Singh naturalised under his second identity. The complaint alleges seven counts for his numerous misrepresentations and unlawful acts that adversely reflect his moral character," the Justice Department said.
The department said it is seeking to revoke the citizenship of Jinchao Wei, a China-born former US Navy sailor convicted of espionage-related offences. According to the Justice Department, Wei enlisted in the Navy in 2021 and by February 2022 had begun conspiring to sell military secrets to China. He became a US citizen in May 2022 under provisions designed to expedite naturalisation for people serving honourably in the US armed forces.
Wei was convicted in August 2025 of conspiracy to commit espionage, espionage and unlawful export of technical data related to defence articles. He was sentenced to 200 months in prison and discharged from the Navy. Among those against whom denaturalisation actions have been initiated are those from Pakistan, Mexico, Cambodia, Nepal and Afghanistan.

The agreement is conditional on Sri Lanka’s Finance Minister presenting the 2027 Budget to Parliament in line with programme parameters and the completion of a financing assurances review to confirm multilateral financing contributions and assess progress on debt restructuring.
Once approved, Sri Lanka will receive SDR 254 million (about $345 million), taking total disbursements under the EFF arrangement to SDR 2.032 billion (about $2.7 billion). The IMF Executive Board approved the four-year arrangement, worth SDR 2.3 billion (about $3 billion), in March 2023.
According to IMF Mission Chief for Sri Lanka Evan Papageorgiou, the economy has remained resilient despite successive shocks. Economic activity grew 4.2 per cent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, marking 11 consecutive quarters of strong growth, while headline inflation stood at 8 per cent in September. Gross official reserves reached $6.9 billion at the end of August, while banks remained well capitalised and profitable.
The IMF said Sri Lanka’s fiscal performance in the first half of 2026 was strong and that its debt restructuring was largely completed.
However, the Fund warned that risks remain tilted to the downside, citing uncertainty over the duration and intensity of the war in the Middle East, global trade policy and the impact of El Niño.
The IMF urged the government to allow domestic fuel prices to adjust in line with international prices and maintain cost-recovery energy pricing while protecting vulnerable households. It called for government support to be targeted, budgeted, carefully costed and time-bound to safeguard fiscal and debt sustainability.
The Fund also recommended strengthening poverty-targeted cash transfers and improving the coverage and responsiveness of Sri Lanka’s social safety nets. If the Middle East conflict generates stronger second-round inflationary pressures, monetary policy should be prepared to tighten to prevent inflation expectations from becoming unanchored.
The IMF said Sri Lanka should maintain momentum on its broader reform agenda, including developing a medium-term revenue strategy, improving the efficiency and fairness of the tax system and strengthening public investment management.
It also called for greater exchange-rate flexibility, preservation of the anti-corruption legislative framework and reforms to liberalise trade, modernise business and labour regulations, expand access to finance and advance digital public infrastructure.

articles.summary: Sri Lanka Development Update  World Bank Group
articles.full_text:
The Sri Lanka Development Update (SLDU) has two main aims. First, it reports on key developments over the past 12 months in Sri Lanka’s economy, places these in longer term and global contexts, and updates the outlook for Sri Lanka’s economy. Second, the SLDU provides a more in-depth examination of selected economic and policy issues. It is intended for a wide audience, including policymakers, business leaders, financial market participants, think tanks, non-governmental organizations and the community of analysts and professionals interested in Sri Lanka’s evolving economy.
Sri Lanka Development Update
SRI LANKA DEVELOPMENT UPDATE (SLDU) - OCTOBER 2026 Edition:
- 
            
            
            From Recovery to TransformationSRI LANKA DEVELOPMENT UPDATE, OCTOBER 2026 Sri Lanka has reached an important milestone in its recovery from the 2022 crisis, with real GDP returning to pre-crisis levels.
The economy expanded by 4.
7 percent in the first half of 2026, marking twelve consecutive quarters of growth and reflecting the benefits of macroeconomic stabilization, fiscal consolidation, exchange rate reforms, and debt restructuring.
Strong industrial activity, investment growth, and resilient services supported the recovery, while fiscal performance significantly exceeded expectations.
Growth is projected at 4.
4 percent in 2026 and 4.
2 percent in 2027.
However, the recovery remains incomplete and uneven.
Poverty, at an estimated 16.
9 percent in 2025, remains well above pre-crisis levels, labor market indicators continue to lag, and renewed inflationary pressures have partially eroded gains in household welfare.
Moving from recovery to transformation will require shifting the growth model toward private investment, exports, and productivity growth.
The report’s special focus examines how agribusiness can become a stronger driver of growth, jobs, exports, and poverty reduction.
While primary agriculture accounts for only 8 percent of GDP, the broader agrifood system contributes about one-sixth of output, over 40 percent of employment, and nearly one-third of merchandise exports.
Despite successes in tea, coconut, cinnamon, seafood, and rubber-based manufacturing, growth remains constrained by policy distortions, weak investment incentives, limited value addition, infrastructure gaps, and restricted access to land and finance.
The report outlines reforms to unlock the sector’s potential and support Sri Lanka’s long-term economic transformation.

- 
            
            
            Weathering the StormSRI LANKA DEVELOPMENT UPDATE, MAY 2026 Sri Lanka’s economy grew an estimated 5 percent in both 2024 and 2025, driven by industry, tourism, exports, and a more-than-20-percent rise in remittances. In November 2025, Cyclone Ditwah flooded nearly a fifth of the country, resulted in over 600 deaths, and created an estimated US$3.4 billion in recovery needs. Growth is projected to moderate to about 3.6 percent in 2026, with downside risks from the Middle East conflict. Buffers have strengthened, but high borrowing costs leave the country exposed. Sustaining the recovery requires reforms that boost private investment and jobs and build resilience.
- 
            
            
            Better Spending for AllSRI LANKA DEVELOPMENT UPDATE, OCTOBER 2025 Sri Lanka’s economy is projected to grow 4.6 percent in 2025, supported by industry and services. The recovery remains uneven: output is still below its 2018 level, and poverty, projected at 22.4 percent, is roughly double its pre-crisis rate. Fiscal space is tight, with over 80 percent of spending tied to salaries, welfare, and interest. The special topic examines how to get more from existing spending through modernized public-sector pay, better capital project planning, and stronger infrastructure maintenance. Durable, inclusive growth also requires macroeconomic stability and reforms to trade, competition, and tax policy.
- 
            
            
            Staying on TrackSRI LANKA DEVELOPMENT UPDATE, APRIL 2025 Sri Lanka’s economy grew 5 percent in 2024, above the 4.4 percent projected, led by industry and services, particularly construction and tourism. Growth is expected to moderate, reflecting lingering crisis scarring, structural impediments, and global trade policy uncertainty. About a third of the population remains poor or at risk of falling back into poverty. A higher, more inclusive growth path will require reforms in trade, investment, competition, and female labor force participation, alongside consistent macro-fiscal and financial policies. Stronger social protection will help ensure the recovery’s benefits reach the most vulnerable.
- 
            
            
            Opening Up to the FutureSRI LANKA DEVELOPMENT UPDATE, OCTOBER 2024 Sri Lanka’s economy stabilized in 2024, with growth expected at 4.4 percent, above earlier forecasts, led by industry and tourism and supported by reforms. The recovery remains fragile and depends on maintaining macroeconomic stability, completing debt restructuring, and sustaining reforms to raise growth and reduce poverty. The special topic argues that Sri Lanka must open further to trade and investment, as exports and investment have underperformed for two decades despite their role in creating better jobs. It sets out priority reforms to remove trade and investment barriers and improve governance, which would raise efficiency, reduce corruption, and strengthen government credibility.
- 
            
            
            Bridge to RecoverySRI LANKA DEVELOPMENT UPDATE, APRIL 2024 The Sri Lankan economy has shown early signs of stabilization with improved fiscal and external balances, supported by a recovery in remittances and tourism and the continued debt service suspension. However, this will be insufficient to reverse crisis-induced welfare losses as poverty levels remain elevated. The narrow path to restoring growth and prosperity will hinge on a successful debt restructuring, adequate support to the most poor and vulnerable, and continued reform implementation despite upcoming elections.
- 
            
            
            Mobilizing Tax Revenue for a Brighter FutureSRI LANKA DEVELOPMENT UPDATE, OCTOBER 2023 Sri Lanka’s longstanding structural weaknesses plunged the country into a severe economic crisis in 2022. The economy has shown initial signs of stabilization, albeit at a low-level equilibrium, in the first half of 2023. Swift and sufficiently deep debt restructuring is needed to restore Sri Lanka’s debt sustainability and regain access to international financial markets.
- 
            
            
            Time to ResetSRI LANKA DEVELOPMENT UPDATE, APRIL 2023 Sri Lanka’s economy was projected to contract 4.3 percent in 2023 amid its deepest economic crisis in decades, with weak demand, job and income losses, and supply constraints weighing on output. More than half a million jobs were lost, and an estimated 2.7 million more people fell into poverty between 2021 and 2022. A slow debt restructuring and limited external financing threatened to prolong the crisis. The SLDU argues this is a structural crisis, not a temporary liquidity shock, requiring deep, permanent fiscal, external, and financial sector reforms and stronger domestic revenue, while protecting the poor and vulnerable throughout the adjustment.
- 
            
            
            Protecting the Poor and Vulnerable in a Time of CrisisSRI LANKA DEVELOPMENT UPDATE, OCTOBER 2022 Sri Lanka’s economic crisis deepened in 2022, as depleted reserves caused severe shortages of fuel, food, and medicine, and unprecedented inflation eroded incomes. After years of fiscal imbalances and unsustainable debt, the country suspended external debt service in April and reached a staff-level agreement with the IMF on a US$2.9 billion facility in September. Poverty doubled to 25.6 percent between 2021 and 2022, pushing 2.7 million more people into poverty. The special focus examines the crisis’s welfare impacts and the role of social protection, calling for fast-tracked structural reforms, stronger social protection, and expanded employment in industry and services.
- 
            
            
            Economic and Poverty Impact of COVID-19SRI LANKA DEVELOPMENT UPDATE, APRIL 2021 Amid the Coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, Sri Lanka’s economy contracted by 3.6 percent in 2020, the worst growth performance on record, as is the case in many countries fighting the pandemic. Swift measures enacted by the government in the second quarter helped contain the first wave of Coronavirus (COVID-19) successfully, but these measures hit sectors like tourism, construction, and transport especially hard, while collapsing global demand impacted the textile industry. Job and earning losses disrupted private consumption and uncertainty impeded investment. As a result, the economy contracted by 16.4 percent (y-o-y) in the second quarter. The economy began to recover in the third quarter as the first wave was brought under control and containment measures were relaxed. The momentum continued in the fourth quarter as the economy was broadly kept open despite a second wave of Coronavirus (COVID-19) infections. The special focus section of this edition discusses the impact of Coronavirus (COVID-19) on poverty in Sri Lanka as of 2021.

(Reuters) -- Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey agreed on Monday to move immediately to implement their collective defense commitments and ensure the "rapid deployment" of agreed military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia, the three countries said in a joint statement shared by Pakistan's foreign ministry.
The decision was taken at an emergency meeting of the Mecca Defense Alliance in Riyadh and would be carried out under "approved arrangements" and the national laws of the three countries, the statement said.
The meeting "reaffirmed the solidarity and unity of our countries in confronting the heinous attacks against the Kingdom and the holy sites," the Saudi defense minister said on X.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Thursday that the Iran-aligned group had attacked a power distribution station in the Saudi city of Medina, which supplies electricity to the Prophet's Mosque, one of Islam's holiest sites.
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
The agreement announced at the time gave no specifics on the military commitments or defense obligations of each country.

The campaign has been led in part by India’s “Cockroach” youth movement, which previously organized street protests that forced the education minister to resign in July.

    Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the poll body's ongoing revision of voter lists. They accuse the revision could disenfranchise millions of voters and benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP. The commission and government deny any wrongdoing.
Here’s what to know:
India is the world’s largest democracy with hundreds of millions of people voting in national and state elections. The Election Commission plays a central role in determining voter eligibility and administering elections, making changes to electoral lists politically significant.
The dispute centers on a nationwide voter list revision known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR. It began last year in the eastern state of Bihar ahead of local elections and has since expanded to most of India’s states and federally administered territories.
Under the process, voters are required to provide documents showing they are eligible to remain on the lists.
The Election Commission says the exercise is needed to remove duplicate and ineligible entries and ensure legitimate voters remain registered. Critics say it could instead exclude legitimate voters, particularly poorer and other vulnerable communities.
They also say the requirements are confusing and difficult for many people to provide, particularly those who lack older government records or other documents.
India’s Election Commission is an independent constitutional body overseeing elections and maintaining voter lists, but opposition parties accuse the commission of favoring Modi's party. They allege the changes could remove people more likely to support opposition parties while preserving or adding voters who favor the BJP.
The BJP and the Election Commission reject the allegations and say the revision has no political motive. Modi's party says the list is being updated to weed out what they call “infiltrators.”
The issue was prominent in West Bengal’s crucial state elections earlier this year after a voter list revision removed about 9 million names, or roughly 12% of the electorate. The deletions left millions of eligible voters unable to cast ballots. Modi’s party won the state for the first time.
Indian law requires a majority vote of commission members to enact changes making disagreements among its members potentially significant.
The Indian Express newspaper reported in September that two of the three election commissioners had formally objected to several decisions involving voter list revisions, registration procedures and the commission’s digital systems.
The newspaper reported Kumar, the election chief, rejected those objections.
The Election Commission said the report reflected “differing views and deliberations” rather than formal written objections.
The “Cockroach” movement, opposition parties and civil society groups have called for Kumar to resign or be removed and for an inquiry into his conduct, including possible criminal proceedings. They want the current revision halted and the previous electoral lists used for future elections.
They also demand a more independent and transparent process for appointing election commissioners.
Election Commission data indicates voter lists in some regions could shrink by as much as 30%, fueling concerns among opposition parties and protest groups over potential exclusions.
The dispute is likely to intensify as the changes resulting from the revision expand throughout India, which is facing a series of state elections early next year.

articles.summary: No missiles, no bullets: US picks 4 new laser, microwave weapons to destroy drone swarms at the speed of  The Times of IndiaSystems Selected for JIATF 401 Directed-Energy Counter-Drone Pilot Program  U.S. Department of War (.gov)US picks four directed-energy weapons for operational testing against drone threats  The Economic TimesAV, Boeing, Epirus And Kord Selected For Directed Energy C-UAS Pilot  Defense DailyPentagon misses deadline on drone lasers, cos...
articles.full_text:
The United States has selected four advanced laser and high powered microwave weapon systems for operational testing as Washington seeks to strengthen its defences against the growing threat posed by drones to military installations and critical infrastructure.
According to the US Department of War, the systems will be evaluated under a directed energy pilot programme led by Joint Interagency Task Force 401, which is tasked with developing and coordinating counter drone capabilities for homeland defence.
The move marks a shift towards testing directed energy weapons in operational environments rather than relying solely on conventional interceptors.
The four systems selected for the pilot programme include AeroVironment’s Palletised High Energy Laser, Epirus’ Leonidas High Powered Microwave system, Kord’s Firefly High Energy Laser and Boeing’s Compact Laser Weapon System.
The systems represent two major forms of directed energy technology being explored by the US military to counter unmanned aerial systems.
How laser and microwave weapons work
High energy laser weapons use concentrated electromagnetic energy to engage drones. The beam is focused on a specific part of the aircraft, delivering enough heat to damage critical components and potentially destroy the target.
The US Army has described directed energy as offering a potentially lower cost per shot and a deeper magazine than conventional kinetic interceptors.
Poll
Do you support the use of directed energy weapons for military defense?
Lasers also operate at the speed of light and do not require conventional ammunition, but their effectiveness depends on maintaining the beam on the target and can be affected by atmospheric conditions and other factors.
High powered microwave(HPM) weapons work differently, using electromagnetic energy to interact with a drone's electronics. The US Office of Naval Research says HPM systems are designed to cause damage or temporary disruption to electronic systems, while their broader beams can allow multiple electronic targets to be engaged simultaneously.
The US Army has tested HPM systems specifically designed to disrupt, disable or destroy multiple unmanned aircraft, making them a complementary layer alongside lasers and conventional counter drone weapons.

articles.title: Pakistan, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia agree to rapid force deployment in the kingdom under Makkah pact - The Financial Express
articles.summary: Pakistan, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia agree to rapid force deployment in the kingdom under Makkah pact  The Financial Express
articles.full_text:
Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye have agreed to deploy military forces and capabilities rapidly in the kingdom, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Monday following an emergency meeting of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Riyadh.
The three countries held an emergency meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC) of the Makkah Defence Alliance to address the security developments and threats facing Saudi Arabia, the FO statement said.
“The committee decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom, in accordance with the approved arrangements and the national legislation of the parties, thereby enhancing readiness, military integration, and the collective capacity to confront and counter threats,” it added.
While the statement did not specifically name any threat, the development comes against the backdrop of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in the Yemen conflict.
In the Riyadh meeting, the three members of the Makkah Defence Alliance condemned “in the strongest terms” the attempted targeting of Makkah and Madina, as well as the continuing attacks targeting cities and civilian and facilities in Saudi Arabia, reaffirming their “unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the kingdom’s security and territorial integrity”, the statement said.
For their part, Pakistan and Turkiye commended the “vigilance and readiness of the Saudi armed forces, as well as the professionalism and high level of competence they have demonstrated in countering the threats and attacks facing the kingdom and in safeguarding its security and territorial integrity”, the FO said.
The SPDC reviewed the outcomes of the political and military consultations preceding the meeting and approved the recommendations submitted to it, affirming that the Makkah pact embodied a firm commitment to collective defence and a unified position in confronting threats, it said.
Moreover, the three countries affirmed that the security of each member of the alliance was an “integral part of the collective security of the three countries, and that translating the Makkah Agreement for Joint Defence into practical measures demonstrates the credibility of the commitment to collective defence, strengthens the effectiveness of deterrence, and reaffirms the unity and determination of our three countries to defend their security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, in accordance with the provisions of the agreement”.
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was part of Pakistan’s delegation in the meeting, joined Geo programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Saath’ via telephone and said Saudi Arabia had made “gains and recovered some areas” in Yemen in the ongoing fighting with the Houthis.
When asked about a possible operational role by Pakistan and Turkiye, the defence minister replied that both nations had a “presence in theatre”, but only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations.
“Whatever assistance they require is being provided. But right now, the Turkish and Pakistani armies are playing a supportive role,” he said, noting that Pakistan was involved in reconnaissance.
The defence minister said the meeting was primarily focused on formalising the Makkah alliance’s operational structure.
“The organisational structure of the alliance was formalised during today’s meeting,” he said.
As part of the institutional development of the Makkah alliance, the SPDC decided to appoint Pakistan’s Lieutenant General (Retd) Nauman Mahmood as the first secretary general of the alliance for a three-year term, the FO statement said.
“The parties welcomed him, wished him every success in the discharge of his duties, and expressed their confidence in his contribution to advancing the alliance and achieving its objectives,” it added.
In an earlier statement on social media platform X, the FO said Pakistan’s delegation to the meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC) included Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and Asif.
“The meeting will also be attended by the respective ministers of foreign affairs, ministers of defence, as well as chiefs of general staff of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and the Republic of Türkiye,” the FO added.
The Makkah defence pact, signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them.
The SPDC meeting under it has been held as Yemen’s Saudi-led coalition government launched a major military campaign on Sunday to recapture territory held by the Houthis.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis showed no signs of abating over the weekend, with the Houthis saying the kingdom had launched dozens of strikes on Yemen’s capital Sanaa, after which they attacked an Aramco facility with ballistic missiles and drones south of Riyadh.
The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait in a lightning offensive.
On Sept 25, the military chiefs of Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia met in Riyadh for urgently convened talks under the pact in light of the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
On Sept 18, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry had expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia, saying Pakistan will go to “any extent” to defend the Gulf state, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”.
Defence Minister Asif also earlier reaffirmed that Pakistan would “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalated.

articles.title: It’s safety first for gas suppliers at semicon inc - ET EnergyWorld
articles.summary: It’s safety first for gas suppliers at semicon inc  ET EnergyWorld
articles.full_text:
Suppliers want updated rules for the storage, transport and handling of toxic and flammable gases as India scales up semiconductor manufacturing, with stakeholders pushing foralignment with global standards.
Suppliers want detailed guidelines from the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO), without which they believe commercial hubs face heightened risk of leaks, fires and process disruption.
This is particularly relevant as manufacturing ecosystem investments at the upcoming Tata fab in Dholera are scaling. Global suppliers such as Linde, Air Liquide and Inox Air Products are preparing infrastructure to service the fab. Additionally, companies such as Merck have signed a partnership with Tata Electronics to provide its full suite of products and services, including advanced gas and chemical delivery systems.
Pioneering work
“Many of these are going to be manufactured in India for the first time. There are a lot of regulatory bodies that create the framework for dealing with cryogenic and hazardous gases, PESO being the leading one,” the supplier added.
Executives say the process could involve around 50 gases, but very few are covered by the prevailing framework.
“We have been made aware of this matter by the industry, and we have asked them to provide us with a list of gases that need to be covered,” said a government official, who did not wish to be named.
Some of the gases are also being imported. “Some will be specialised gases that India has not imported before; so, these bodies need regulations to be in place soon to keep pace with the ambition,” the executive added.
Adopting international safety standards will help protect workers, secure supply chains, and build investor confidence, stakeholders said. The view is that India’s semiconductor ambitions will require a supporting ecosystem to move in lockstep with the fab and packaging facilities themselves.
Industrial and electronic specialty gases are a critical part of this ecosystem, with applications across wafer fabrication, deposition, etching, cleaning, atmosphere control, packaging, assembly and testing.
“We are looking at the standards that are in place in other countries that have more mature semiconductor manufacturing operations to understand best practices that we can adopt,” said the government official. “The industry’s own standards in this regard are quite exhaustive and are being reviewed as well.”
India Electronics and Semiconductor Association (IESA) said some critical gases required for semiconductor manufacturing, helium, silane, phosphine, diborane and arsine, are not currently made in India.
Others, such as hydrogen, argon, and ammonia, are made in India but do not meet the required purity levels.
In addition, some highly specialised gases will be used once fabs are operational, requiring specialised standards.
Diganta Sarma, head of business development & strategy at Inox Air Products, said semiconductor manufacturing requires gases at extremely stringent purity levels, along with specialised requirements for their packaging, testing, storage, transportation and handling.
“As newer semiconductor processes and electronic speciality gases are introduced at scale in India, the regulatory framework will need to continuously evolve to address these applications,” Sarma said. “India should progressively benchmark its framework against globally accepted practices across the complete electronic-gases value chain, from purity specifications and analytical testing to packaging, cylinder and container compatibility, storage, transportation, gas-detection systems and safe handling.”
Greater alignment with globally accepted practices would also make it easier for semiconductor manufacturers operating in India to integrate their local facilities with overseas manufacturing and supply chains, Sarma said.
Ashok Chandak, president, SEMI India and IESA, concurred. He said India shouldalign its semiconductor-gas ecosystem with SEMI global standards rather than develop a parallel India-specific regime with a simple objective: Global standards, Indian manufacturing capability, and uncompromised safety.
“India should avoid creating a parallel semiconductor-gas standards regime,” he said. “The global semiconductor industry already has a strong standards framework through SEMI, including SEMI C3 for gas specifications and analytical procedures. BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards), PESO, the Ministry of Electronics and information technology/India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) and industry should work together to harmonise Indian requirements with these global benchmarks, while PESO continues to focus on the critical areas of safety, storage, transportation and handling of hazardous gases.”
He said the country needs a three-layer framework: BIS for Indian standards and testing methods, PESO for safety and hazardous-gas handling, and SEMI for semiconductor-grade gas specifications and industry best practices. “BIS already has a committee whose scope explicitly includes high-purity speciality gases and gas mixtures.PESO’s role is very important, but it should not necessarily be the body that defines semiconductor gas purity specifications,” he said.

articles.title: Almost no locomotives left: How Russia's strikes are choking Ukraine's lifeline - India Today
articles.summary: Almost no locomotives left: How Russia's strikes are choking Ukraine's lifeline  India Today
articles.full_text:
Ukraine is seeking locomotives and funds as Russian strikes hammer its railways, ports and industry. The damage is choking exports, shrinking tax revenue and raising the cost of sustaining the war.
More than four years into Russia's full-scale invasion, Ukraine is facing a deepening economic squeeze. Russian strikes are battering factories, ports, railways and bridges across the country. At the same time, the cost of fighting continues to rise. Kyiv is now scrambling for money to sustain the war -- and for locomotives to keep its economy moving.
Russian strikes on Ukraine's rail network have destroyed or damaged hundreds of locomotives, putting further pressure on a transport system already stretched by the war.
The impact is now reaching the country's Black Sea trade. Grain, iron ore and other cargo still need to travel from inland production centres to the ports, meaning damaged maritime infrastructure is only part of the problem. Without enough trains to haul freight, getting cargo to the berths could become the major bottleneck.
Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi told the Financial Times that Ukraine is negotiating with European countries whose railways use the same track gauge in an effort to secure additional locomotives and rolling stock.
The urgency is particularly clear around the port of Pivdennyi, one of Ukraine's major maritime gateways. Mykyta Hrubov, chief executive of port operator TIS, told the FT that three locomotives had been lost around the company's terminal.
"There is a big shortage now, this is a weak point for us," he said, as per the report.
RUSSIA IS HUNTING UKRAINE'S TRAINS
The locomotive shortage is not simply the result of ageing equipment or battlefield attrition. Russia has increasingly made Ukraine's railway system a target.
Russian forces have stepped up attacks on trains carrying grain and iron ore, two of the country's most important export commodities. Earlier reports said more than 500 locomotives had been damaged or destroyed since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022, with more than half of those losses occurring in 2026.
Ukraine's railway operator has also warned that it is losing dozens of locomotives every month.
The attacks are no longer confined to the frontline. Russia has increasingly deployed jet-powered drones to hunt moving trains, using relay networks that allow operators to control the drones even when Ukrainian electronic warfare systems are trying to disrupt them.
Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, chairman of the management board at Ukraine's state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia, has said the campaign goes beyond disrupting military logistics.
"Russians aim to isolate our frontline communities, sow panic and fear among the already exhausted locals, paralyze the economy," he said.
The railway is also essential for evacuating civilians and transporting critical supplies, meaning every locomotive lost has consequences well beyond the movement of commercial cargo.
Ukraine's 1,520-millimetre railway gauge makes the replacement effort harder. Most European railways use the narrower 1,435-millimetre standard, limiting the number of locomotives that can be transferred and put into service quickly.
THE PORTS ARE UNDER PRESSURE TOO
The railway crisis is colliding with another major problem: Russia's intensifying attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea export infrastructure.
Ukraine's Black Sea ports have long been crucial to keeping its economy moving. Before the full-scale invasion, they handled the vast majority of the country's grain exports. Now repeated attacks have damaged port infrastructure and disrupted the routes connecting farms and industrial sites to the coast.
The consequences are already being felt by farmers and exporters.
Ukraine had expected to export tens of millions of tonnes of agricultural products this year, but the disruption to maritime routes has sharply reduced the amount that can reach overseas markets. The longer the ports remain constrained, the greater the pressure on alternative routes.
But alternative routes are expensive and limited.
That makes locomotives a big part of the problem. A port may have the capacity to load a vessel, but that capacity is of little use if grain and iron ore cannot be moved from inland Ukraine to the docks.
The disruption is also creating a storage problem for farmers, who risk being forced to keep harvests in temporary storage or sell at lower prices when transport and export options disappear.
UKRAINE'S WAR BILL IS RISING
The pressure on transport infrastructure is unfolding against a much larger fiscal crisis.
In Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Russian airstrikes have brought major parts of the city's steel and mining industry to a standstill. The industrial city of about 600,000 people is now trying to preserve basic services while its economic base contracts.
Mayor Oleksandr Vilkul said the city was doing everything possible to keep hospitals open, schools and kindergartens functioning and buses running.
"In Kryvyi Rih, the situation is actually worse than anywhere else, apart from the front line itself," Vilkul, a former mining executive, said in a video address.
The city's largest employer, ArcelorMittal's mining and steel complex, suspended operations last month after a series of Russian ballistic missile strikes. The damage reflects a broader collapse across an industry that once accounted for about a tenth of Ukraine's economic output.
Steel plants in other industrial centres, including Zaporizhzhia, have also been forced to halt or sharply reduce production.
"It's about survival. Right now, we need to survive," Vilkul said.
The damage is translating directly into lost tax revenue at a time when the government needs more money than ever.
UKRAINE'S REVENUE SHRINKS
Ukraine spent more than USD 44 billion on defence during the first nine months of this year alone, according to Reuters. Over the same period, the government raised about USD 42 billion in tax revenue.
Russian attacks have made that imbalance worse. Pidlasa said Ukraine's budget had lost more than 49.5 billion hryvnias, or about USD 1.1 billion, in tax revenue during the first nine months of the year because strikes damaged property, disrupted logistics and forced businesses to shut temporarily.
The cumulative loss could reach 70 billion hryvnias by the end of the year, according to government estimates.
The financial pressure is already shaping Ukraine's plans for next year. The government has proposed a record defence budget of about USD 110 billion, excluding direct military assistance from allies. Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko has estimated that the unfunded gap for next year is already more than USD 32 billion.
Marchenko has argued that frozen Russian assets in Europe could help plug the hole. EU countries have immobilised roughly 210 billion euros in Russian central bank assets since the invasion.
"Ukraine continues to mobilise domestic resources, but the scale of Russia's war puts clear limits on our capacity," Marchenko said on X.
For Ukrainian businesses, the uncertainty is becoming harder to absorb.
Some companies have cut back operations, while others have shelved investment plans. The agriculture sector faces a similar squeeze. Russian attacks on Black Sea ports have disrupted one of Ukraine's biggest sources of export revenue, while the shortage of locomotives threatens the inland supply chain needed to move crops and raw materials to the coast.
That leaves Ukraine facing a problem that is both military and economic: it needs money to replace the infrastructure being destroyed, but the destruction itself is reducing the tax and export revenues needed to fund the war.
For the railways, there is no plan to stop. Pertsovskyi said Ukrzaliznytsia was preparing for multiple scenarios and working on alternatives, including moving passengers by road when trains are hit.
"We have various operational plans to balance safety, but we are certainly not considering a scenario where we stop. Just as our country does not contemplate giving up the fight, the railway, naturally, does not contemplate halting its operations," he said, as quoted by Politico.
There is little sign of the pressure easing. Peace talks remain deadlocked, while Russia has said it will continue targeting Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. For a country already struggling to keep its economy afloat, every new strike brings more damage to infrastructure, disrupts trade and puts further strain on public finances, which only adds to the already heavy cost of a war with no end in sight.

articles.title: India’s Highway Reset: Gadkari Unveils Roadmap for Safer, Greener Roads - Indianmasterminds
articles.summary: India’s Highway Reset: Gadkari Unveils Roadmap for Safer, Greener Roads  Indianmasterminds
articles.full_text:
New Delhi: Union Road Transport and Highways Minister Nitin Gadkari inaugurated Chintan Shivir 2026, a two-day national conclave focused on making India’s highway infrastructure safer, greener and more efficient.
Held at Tent City 2 in Ekta Nagar, Narmada district, the conclave brings together state transport and PWD ministers, senior officials, implementing agencies and other stakeholders under the theme “Gatishakti se Pragati.”
Focus on Better Highway Planning
Gadkari stressed that highway projects need stronger preparation at the Detailed Project Report (DPR) stage.
He highlighted the importance of proper surveys, alignment planning, land acquisition, utility shifting and statutory clearances before construction begins. Better preparation, he said, can reduce project delays, cost escalation and implementation problems.
The minister also called for states to share successful practices and field-level solutions so that effective models can be replicated across the country.
Road Safety to Be Built Into Highway Design
Road safety was another major focus of the conclave.
Gadkari said accident-prone locations should be identified early and appropriate safety measures incorporated during highway planning and construction rather than addressed only after projects become operational.
The approach is aimed at improving highway design while reducing road accidents and making travel safer for road users.
Green and Sustainable Highways
The conclave also places significant emphasis on environmental sustainability.
Gadkari called for wider use of environment-friendly construction methods, recycled materials and innovative technologies to improve highway quality while reducing construction and maintenance costs.
A document on Environment & Wildlife Mitigation Measures was launched during the inaugural session, highlighting the need to protect the environment and wildlife while developing transport infrastructure.
Technology and Tolling Reforms
Technology-driven reforms also feature prominently in the two-day discussions.
The minister highlighted initiatives such as the FASTag Annual Pass and Multi-Lane Free Flow (MLFF), which are aimed at modernising toll collection, improving traffic movement and making highway travel more convenient.
The conclave will also examine ways to use new technologies and cost-effective materials to improve construction and maintenance.
Key Areas Under Discussion
The two-day Chintan Shivir will cover several major aspects of highway development, including:
- PM GatiShakti and integrated infrastructure planning
- Land acquisition and Bhoomi Rashi
- Model Concession Agreements and ratings
- Safe and green highway design
- Road safety and toll reforms
- Quality assurance and project monitoring
A BRICS Compendium on Perspectives in Sustainable Transport was also launched, adding an international perspective to discussions on sustainable mobility.
Highways as Drivers of Economic Growth
Gadkari underlined the wider economic importance of highway infrastructure, noting that modern roads need to provide seamless connectivity between cities, towns, ports, markets and industrial centres.
Better connectivity can support trade, investment, employment and economic activity by improving the movement of people and goods.
The conclave therefore aims to bring the Centre, states and implementing agencies together to address practical challenges that affect the timely delivery of major infrastructure projects.
Centre-State Collaboration at the Core
A key objective of Chintan Shivir 2026 is to strengthen cooperation between the Centre and states.
Rather than focusing only on policy discussions, the conclave is intended to provide a platform for officials and implementing agencies to exchange field-level experiences, identify common problems and develop solutions that can be applied across different regions.
The discussions are expected to focus on improving project planning, monitoring, quality, safety and sustainability.
The broader objective is to create a highway network that can meet India’s growing mobility and economic requirements while incorporating technology, environmental responsibility and stronger safety standards.

articles.title: RBI expected to hike interest rate, but will it be an effective way to contain inflation? - The Times of India
articles.summary: RBI expected to hike interest rate, but will it be an effective way to contain inflation?  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
By Apoorva Javadekar, Chief Economist at Shriram Group
When the RBI's bulletin, published ten days ahead of its October Monetary Policy meeting, carries a chart titled "Broad-Based Uptick in CPI Headline Inflation", the direction of travel for interest rates is hardly a mystery. And the case for a rate hike, at least on the surface, is straightforward.
Consumer inflation has risen to 4.8% in August, well above the RBI's 4% target, driven by food prices at 5.95% and Brent crude surging back to $105/bbl from July lows of $70/bbl, a direct consequence of the US-Iran stalemate. Crude at these levels almost certainly alters the RBI's inflation trajectory and risks broadening price pressures beyond food and fuel: already, 40% of CPI basket items are tracking above 4%, up from 32% in July. Household inflation expectations, per the RBI's own surveys, have risen steadily since February and the RBI would like to keep them anchored by acting on time.
And a robust 7.8% GDP print in Q1 FY27, corroborated by resilient high-frequency indicators through September, provides the RBI with the growth buffer to prioritise inflation without undue concern about choking the recovery. With real interest rates compressed to just 0.4% in August, against a pre-COVID average of 2.1%, the RBI will also be concerned about the risk of artificially cheap credit fuelling inefficient booms, adding one more argument for tightening.
Yet the case for an aggressive, prolonged rate hike cycle is considerably more fragile upon closer examination.
To begin with, the inflation trajectory, at least until now, has largely tracked the RBI's own projected path. Unless crude prices durably reset the RBI's forward expected inflation trajectory, it is difficult to justify a hike now that the RBI itself did not deem necessary when it published its August projections consistent with the current levels.
Moreover, the top ten contributing items still account for roughly 50% of August's inflation print, similar to the concentration observed over the past few months, suggesting the uptick remains supply-driven and item-specific rather than broad-based.
Second, rate hikes carry real costs for the growth drivers that matter most. Capital expenditure - one of the primary engines of India's recent GDP performance - is acutely rate-sensitive, and a prolonged tightening cycle risks derailing corporate investment plans, particularly within the MSME sector. Exports, the other growth pillar, already face the overhang of potential 100% US tariffs linked to India's Russian oil purchases.
Third, India's household sector is acutely vulnerable to rate hikes: household debt has risen to 45% of GDP from 36% pre-COVID, and with the banking system having largely migrated from fixed to floating rate loans, rate hikes transmit rapidly and simultaneously into new credit costs and rising EMIs on existing loans, further compressing disposable incomes precisely when food and fuel inflation are already doing the same.
Finally, the rainfall deficit, while real at 15%, may prove less inflationary than feared. Sowing is only 1.6% below last year's levels, and the Food Corporation of India holds larger-than-usual rice and wheat buffers that can meaningfully smooth prices of these key staples.
The more significant risk from deficient rainfall is to growth, not inflation: over the past fifteen years, non-deficit years have delivered 4.6% crop GVA growth against a contraction of 1.3% in deficit years. And displaced agricultural workers flooding non-farm labour markets tend to depress wages and incomes well beyond the farm gate even for the non-farm sector.
An important policy question is should the RBI hike in response to the Fed, ECB, and BOJ? The prevailing narrative holds that it should, for fear that narrowing rate differentials will trigger capital outflows and put the INR under pressure.
The case for hiking because of the Fed-hike is however, weak as I argue next: India's policy rates are already among the highest in Asia; regional peers Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia held rates at their most recent meetings, leaving India's relative rate advantage intact; $785bn in FX reserves provide ample capacity to manage INR volatility; and the rupiah weakened despite Indonesia's unscheduled May hike, while the won stayed resilient despite a negative rate differential, driven instead by strong export growth.
Rate hikes, it turns out, are an unreliable instrument for managing currency pressures rooted in global risk sentiment.
This leaves the MPC confronting two questions that cut to the heart of the debate. First, do rate hikes meaningfully contain inflation that is fundamentally supply-driven - in food, fuel?
And second, if a prolonged tightening cycle is too costly to sustain in terms of growth, what is the ultimate purpose of a shallow 50-basis-point hike - beyond signalling intent? The answers to these questions, more than any single data point, should guide the October decision.
